question: Apart from preventing overfitting, are there any side effects (desirable or otherwise) of applying dropout in deep neural networks?

sections.title: Background: what dropout is
sections.text: Dropout was introduced in 2012 as a technique to avoid overfitting [1] and was subsequently applied in the 2012 winning submission for the Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge [1]. In its standard form, each neuron is omitted with probability p during training, and once trained the full network is used, with neuron outputs scaled by the keep probability to compensate for the larger network [1]. The canonical explanation of the method is that it reduces feature co-adaptation, i.e., the situation in which the outputs of individual neurons provide useful information only in combination with other neuron outputs [1]. Srivastava et al. (2014) proposed dropout as a cheap way of preventing neural networks from overfitting, and the result sparked large interest in studying and extending the algorithm [2]. This report surveys the documented side effects of applying dropout — the consequences beyond the plain prevention of overfitting — and separates the desirable from the undesirable.

snippets: Dropout was introduced in 2012 as a technique to avoid overfitting [1] and was subsequently applied in the 2012 winning submission for the Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that revitalized deep neural network research [2].

Standard dropout is equivalent to adding an additional layer after a layer of neurons that simply sets values to zero with some probability during training, and multiplies them by $1 - p$ during testing.
Hinton et al. [1] showed that standard dropout reduces feature co-adaptation, where the outputs of individual neurons only provide useful information in combination with other neuron outputs.

sections.title: Side effect 1: an implicit weight-sharing ensemble, and a train/test asymmetry
sections.text: Randomly dropping neurons creates an exponential number of possible thinned networks, and dropout was interpreted from the start as implicitly averaging over this ensemble: for a single hidden layer with N units, the network's softmax output is equivalent to the geometric mean of the outputs of the 2^N possible networks under dropout [1]. This differs from bagging in that only one model is trained and test-time inference uses an approximation to the geometric mean rather than an arithmetic average [1]. In dropout the many subnetworks share a single global set of weights, whereas in a conventional ensemble each member has its own parameters [3]. Equivalently, dropout training effectively trains many neural networks that share most of their weights [4]. This ensemble reading is arguably more plausible than the Bayesian one when dropout rates are not tuned to the data, since any sensible approximation to the true Bayesian posterior must depend on the training data [5]. The ensemble side effect has concrete test-time consequences: stochasticity is not always desired at test time, so the weights are scaled down by the keep probability and every weight participates, and the resulting deterministic single-network prediction differs only minimally from full Monte-Carlo model averaging [4]. If the posterior predictive is instead approximated by T stochastic forward passes, the standard deployment simply patches the train/test asymmetry with weight scaling rather than with sampling [4].

snippets: In the original dropout paper, Hinton et al. [1] observe that there is a large number of possible neural network structures that result from randomly dropping neurons, and suggest that dropout implicitly performs averaging over this ensemble of possible networks. For instance, using a network with a single hidden layer of $N$ units and softmax activation is equivalent to taking the geometric mean of the outputs of the $2^{N}$ possible networks under dropout [1].

Standard dropout training varies from bagging in that only one model is trained, and an approximation to the geometric mean of the dropout ensemble's outputs is used rather than an arithmetic mean [28].

snippets: Dropout makes the neural network stochastic. During training, this behavior is desired since this effectively trains many neural networks that share most of the weights.

The stochasticity isn't always desired at test time. In order to make it deterministic, the weights are scaled down by multiplying by $p$ . That is, every weight that once was dropped out during training will be used at test time, but its magnitude is scaled down to account for the fact that it used to be not present during training.

When a regular neural network has dropouts, it's possible to approximate the posterior predictive distribution by performing $T$ stochastic forward passes and averaging the results. This is called “Monte-Carlo dropout” [6]. In practice, the difference between the Monte-Carlo model averaging and weight scaling is minimal. However, we can use the variance or entropy of the results of $T$ stochastic forward passes to estimate the model uncertainty.

sections.title: Side effect 2: implicit weight decay and weight sparsity (toward compression)
sections.text: Dropout also behaves as an implicit weight regularizer. The expectation of the dropout gradient with respect to a network weight is approximately the gradient of the subnetwork ensemble regularized by an adaptive weight decay, and an alternative interpretation treats dropout training as adaptive weight decay by viewing dropout as feature noising in generalized linear models [6]. Surveys of dropout theory accordingly list dropout as a weight-regularization method, alongside its ensemble, Bayesian, and data-augmentation readings [1]. A related structural side effect is sparsification: standard dropout promotes sparsity in the weights, causing more weights to be near zero [1]. This side effect has been exploited deliberately — dropout methods are now applied to compress deep neural networks, and model compression is counted among dropout's main applications alongside regularization and uncertainty measurement [1].

sections.title: Side effect 3: dropout as implicit data augmentation
sections.text: Dropout can also be read as data augmentation. Using dropout in a network can be interpreted as a kind of data augmentation in the input space without domain knowledge: the dropout noise can be projected back into the input space to generate augmented versions of the training data, and training a deterministic network on the augmented samples yields similar results [7]. The underlying hypothesis is that noise-based regularization increases training-data coverage at every hidden layer [7]. Later work likewise describes dropout as an implicit form of sophisticated data augmentation that increases training-data coverage, e.g., inducing translations, rotations, and scalings for image data [8].

snippets: Dropout is typically interpreted as bagging a large number of models sharing parameters. We show that using dropout in a network can also be interpreted as a kind of data augmentation in the input space without domain knowledge.

We hypothesize that noise based regularization techniques result in a similar effect of increasing training data coverage at every hidden layer and this work presents multiple experimental observations to support our hypothesis.

sections.title: Side effect 4: structured noise that steers optimization to flatter minima
sections.text: Dropout changes where gradient-based optimization lands, not just how regularized the solution is. Training with dropout is equivalent to training with a specific noise, and the implicit regularization behind that noise structure finds solutions with better generalization [9]. Gradient descent with dropout selects flatter minima than standard gradient descent, and flatter minima are widely associated with better generalization and stability [9]. The dropout noise is anisotropic: its variance is larger in the sharper directions of the loss landscape, and the Hessian of the loss at the found minima aligns with the noise covariance matrix [9]. A complementary theoretical account derives an implicit regularization of dropout that (i) condenses the input weights of hidden neurons onto a few isolated orientations and (ii) leads to flatter minima; since condensation reduces the network's complexity, dropout may help generalization by constraining the model's complexity [10].

snippets: Similar to SGD, training with dropout is equivalent to that with some specific noise. The implicit regularization behind this specific noise structure finds solutions with better generalization (Hinton et al., 2012; Srivastava et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2020).

We show that compared with the standard gradient descent (GD), the GD with dropout selects flatter minima. As suggested by many existing works (Keskar et al., 2016; Neyshabur et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2018), flatter minima are more likely to have better generalization and stability.

We further find that the variance of a noise induced by the dropout is larger at the sharper direction of the loss landscape and the Hessian of the loss landscape at the found minima aligns with the noise covariance matrix

sections.title: Side effect 5 (desirable): dropout as a source of uncertainty estimates
sections.text: The most-cited desirable side effect is that dropout training doubles as approximate Bayesian inference. Gal and Ghahramani cast dropout training as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes, showing that the dropout objective minimizes the KL divergence between an approximate distribution and the posterior of a deep Gaussian process [11]. A direct result is a tool for modeling uncertainty with dropout networks — extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far — without sacrificing computational complexity or test accuracy [11]. Operationally, Monte Carlo (MC) dropout keeps dropout on at test time and approximates the posterior predictive by averaging T stochastic forward passes; the variance or entropy of those passes then estimates model uncertainty [4]. MC dropout is a cheap approximate inference technique that obtains uncertainty by performing dropout at test time [12], and dropout's uncertainty improved predictive log-likelihood and RMSE over prior state of the art, with a further application to reinforcement learning, where uncertainty over the agent's Q-value function enables faster learning via Thompson sampling [11]. Because good uncertainty estimates can be cheaply obtained from common dropout models, heavier variational-inference machinery may amount to unnecessary additional computation [11].

snippets: In this paper we develop a new theoretical framework casting dropout training in deep neural networks (NNs) as approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes.

A direct result of this theory gives us tools to model uncertainty with dropout NNs – extracting information from existing models that has been thrown away so far. This mitigates the problem of representing uncertainty in deep learning without sacrificing either computational complexity or test accuracy.

We show that the dropout objective, in effect, minimises the Kullback-Leibler divergence between an approximate distribution and the posterior of a deep Gaussian process (marginalised over its finite rank covariance function parameters).
We show a considerable improvement in predictive log-likelihood and RMSE compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and finish by using dropout's uncertainty in deep reinforcement learning.
With uncertainty estimates over the agent's Q-value function, techniques such as Thompson sampling (Thompson, 1933) can be used to learn much faster.
Given that good uncertainty estimates can be cheaply obtained from common dropout models, this might result in unnecessary additional computation.
citations.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning

sections.title: Side effect 6 (undesirable): uncertainty that is miscalibrated or overconfident
sections.text: The uncertainty side effect comes with known limitations. Confidence estimates computed with a naive implementation of dropout can be poorly calibrated, particularly when using convolutional networks [12]. Even with its improvements over deterministic networks, MC dropout can still produce over-confident predictions [12]. The structured-dropout work explains this through the ensemble lens: confidence calibration is related to the diversity of the models sampled with dropout, and the poor calibration of MC dropout is attributed to limited model diversity; promoting diversity with structured dropout yields better calibrated confidence [12]. Independent comparisons report that MC dropout can be overconfident and that deep ensembles usually outperform it on out-of-distribution benchmarks [13]; deep ensembles have been shown to generate well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and to significantly outperform (or match) MC-dropout [5]. Practitioners likewise note that the uncertainties estimated with MC dropout need to be calibrated, in contrast to deep ensembles [14].

snippets: Dropout, a commonly used training technique, has recently been linked to Bayesian inference, yielding an efficient way to quantify uncertainty in neural network models. However, as previously demonstrated, confidence estimates computed with a naive implementation of dropout can be poorly calibrated, particularly when using convolutional networks.
Despite improvements over deterministic NNs, it has been noted that MC dropout can still produce over-confident predictions [25].

Inspired by [25], we view MC dropout as an ensemble of models sampled with dropout. We show that confidence calibration is related to model diversity in an ensemble, and attribute the poor calibration of MC dropout to limited model diversity.

sections.title: Side effect 7 (undesirable): theoretical pathologies of the Bayesian reinterpretation
sections.text: Reading dropout as variational Bayesian inference is itself not without problems. The framework suffers from undefined or pathological behaviour of the true posterior related to the use of improper priors, and from an ill-defined variational objective due to the singularity of the approximating distribution relative to the true posterior [2]. Concretely, the log-uniform prior of variational Gaussian dropout generally does not induce a proper posterior, so the reported sparsification cannot be explained by standard Bayesian or minimum-description-length arguments and falls into the same non-Bayesian category as the Lasso [2]. As a consequence, the approximate uncertainty estimates do not have their usual interpretation, and the model may still exhibit overfitting [2]. In short, the 'dropout is a Bayesian model' side effect carries a caveat: parts of the Bayesian reading are less defensible than the ensemble reading.

snippets: We show that the proposed framework suffers from several issues; from undefined or pathological behaviour of the true posterior related to use of improper priors, to an ill-defined variational objective due to singularity of the approximating distribution relative to the true posterior.

As we describe in Section 3, the log uniform prior introduced in (Kingma et al., 2015) generally does not induce a proper posterior, and thus the reported sparsification (Molchanov et al., 2017) cannot be explained by the standard Bayesian and the related minimum description length (MDL) arguments. In this sense, sparsification via variational inference with log uniform prior falls into the same category of non-Bayesian approaches as, for example, Lasso (Tibshirani, 1996).
Specifically, the approximate uncertainty estimates do not have the usual interpretation, and the model may exhibit overfitting.
citations.title: Variational Bayesian dropout: pitfalls and fixes

sections.title: Side effect 8 (undesirable): slower convergence, reduced capacity, and inference overhead
sections.text: On the practical side, dropout has measurable costs. It typically increases the number of training iterations required for convergence, since only the weights of the active neurons are updated in each optimization step [15]. Due to the randomness in the architecture, it increases the convergence time; as a regularizer it reduces the effective capacity of the model, so one must increase the size of the model to compensate for the missed units [16]. Dropout also sacrifices training accuracy, since the entire network is not used during training, while improving validation accuracy [17]. At test time, exploiting the uncertainty side effect requires multiple stochastic forward passes — e.g., T = 100 passes through the trained model in one study [18] — and multi-run uncertainty estimation in general creates efficiency issues for real-time deployment [18].

sections.title: Side effect 9 and synthesis: robustness-related uses, and the overall balance
sections.text: There is one more functional side effect: dropout has been proposed as a way to defend against adversarial examples, on the view that it regularizes the network by adding noise to its hidden units [19]. More broadly, dropout methods have expanded well beyond their original overfitting role, with network compression and Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty measurement among their main applications [1]. Taken together, the evidence answers the question affirmatively. Beyond preventing overfitting, dropout (a) implicitly trains an exponentially large weight-sharing ensemble, creating a train/test asymmetry that standard deployments patch with weight scaling [1][3][4]; (b) acts as an implicit adaptive weight decay and induces weight sparsity usable for compression [6][1]; (c) behaves as implicit data augmentation [7]; (d) steers optimization toward flatter minima and condensed weights [9][10]; (e) provides cheap Bayesian-style uncertainty estimates, useful, e.g., for exploration in reinforcement learning [11]; and (f) has been leveraged for robustness to adversarial perturbations [19]. The undesirable side effects are: slower convergence and reduced effective model capacity [15][16], the sacrifice of training accuracy [17], test-time inference overhead when dropout is kept on [18], uncertainty estimates that are often poorly calibrated or overconfident relative to deep ensembles [12][13], and theoretical pathologies of the variational-Bayesian reading [2].

question: Are there papers that use different formats of Q&A with the user to clarify intent and compose more complicated prompts to LLM?

sections.title: Short answer: yes — two complementary research threads
sections.text:
Yes. There is a substantial and active body of literature in which a system interacts with the user through structured clarification Q&A to resolve intent ambiguity and then uses the clarified intent to compose a more complex or better-specified prompt, query, or instruction for a large language model (LLM). This work organizes into two complementary threads.

The first thread, clarification question generation (CQG), formalized the task of generating clarifying questions to disambiguate user intent in information-seeking systems, together with a taxonomy of clarification types derived from large-scale search logs and multiple question-generation models [1]. Subsequent work studied specific question formats — yes/no questions [2], multiple-choice questions [3][33] — and the policy of when to ask: clarity prediction [6], Bayesian ambiguity quantification [22], cost-aware gating [19], and fixed interaction budgets [32] — as well as how to learn question selection, via reinforcement learning [5] or retrieval of discriminative questions [4].

The second thread emerged with LLMs, in which clarification dialogue is used to elicit latent user intent so the system can compose a better prompt or task specification before acting. An agent has been trained to ask strategic questions to close the so-called 'intention expression gap' between a user's high-dimensional mental model and what the user can write as an instruction [8]; reinforcement-learning agents proactively clarify latent intent for open-ended deep research [12]; and instructive search interfaces prompt users to clarify vague requests so that clarifying turns 'help users refine their goals and produce more focused queries' [28]. Surveys now treat clarification questions as a standard response to ambiguous or underspecified input [30][31], and controlled studies directly compare clarification-based prompt construction against alternative prompt-improvement strategies such as checklist-guided rewriting [25].

sections.title: Formats of clarification Q&A studied in the literature
sections.text:
The literature distinguishes and explicitly manipulates several formats of clarification questions. The original CQG task, introduced for open-domain information seeking, was accompanied by 'a clarification type taxonomy based a large-scale search log analysis' and three generation models, including a rule-based template selection and slot-filling model and a neural question generator [1]. Yes/no (closed) clarifying questions have been studied as a low-effort format: they make it easier for the system to decide when to show retrieval results, and affirmative answers increase confidence in the retrieval; a BERT-based model was evaluated on the Qulac dataset [2]. Multiple-choice clarification is also a studied format: QuestBench argues that 'the multiple-choice format for evaluating question-asking is a necessary precursor to open-ended formats' and considers how easy clarifying questions are for users to answer [3]. In text-to-SQL, one system uses 'in-context learning to detect ambiguous phrases, classify them, and generate targeted clarification questions with multiple-choice options for query rewriting' [17][33]. Suggestion-style turns, where the system offers candidate interpretations for the user to pick among, appear in position work on instructive search interfaces, e.g., the follow-up 'Do you mean for the environment, for health, or for animals?' [28].

Alongside the question format, a second design question is when to ask. Clarity can be predicted without supervision from retrieved-item coherency, so that only ambiguous queries trigger a clarifying question [6]. CLEAR-KGQA uses Bayesian inference 'to quantify query ambiguity and guide LLMs in determining when and how to request clarification from users' [22]. Data-Aware Socratic Guidance (DASG) treats dialogue as an optimization decision and asks clarifying questions only under an explicit cost–benefit condition [19]. Ambig-IAC operates under a fixed interaction budget, generating a series of clarification questions that narrow the set of valid configurations [32]. Learned selection of clarifying questions has also been explored, including reinforcement learning over clarification dialogue to maximize recall of the potential intents of an ambiguous query [5], and retrieval of discriminative clarifying questions for task-oriented intent disambiguation [4]. The practice predates LLMs: in the CoSQL conversational text-to-SQL benchmark, an ambiguous question 'will receive clarification questions or notice to rephrase' from the expert [7]. A survey of LLM knowledge boundaries likewise lists 'asking clarification questions' as a common strategy for unknown knowledge, citing a cluster of dedicated works [31].

sections.title: Using clarification to compose better prompts and instructions for the LLM
sections.text:
In the LLM era, clarification dialogue is used explicitly as a step before — or part of — prompt and instruction composition. The Nous agent addresses the 'intention expression gap', 'the difficulty for humans to effectively convey complex, high-dimensional thoughts to AI': it reframes the problem 'from passive instruction following a Socratic collaboration paradigm', where the agent 'formulates strategic questions to systematically resolve its uncertainty about the user's goal', and trains the inquiry policy with an information-theoretic reward equivalent to Shannon-entropy reduction over the space of task specifications [8]. IntentRL trains proactive agents 'to clarify latent user intent' for open-ended deep research, building a 'Clarification Directed Acyclic Graph (C-DAG) that maps queries to both shallow (surface-level) and deep (rubric-derived) intents' so that the clarified intent drives the research process [12]. An AI assistant for intentional digital living uses a system prompt in which the assistant 'engages in a multi-turn conversation to better understand the user's intention', with the per-turn goal to 'ask one clarification question to make the intention specific and actionable' [11]. The PRIHA primary-care assistant, a RAG-enhanced LLM framework, proactively asks clarifying questions in multiple rounds whenever a query is flagged as complex, e.g., clarifying the actual meaning of 'better' in 'Where to find a better dental clinic' [27]. In image generation, a proactive text-to-image agent 'tackles prompt underspecification by asking clarifying questions and maintaining an editable belief graph of user intent, thereby converging on the desired image through multiturn interactions' [29].

The ask-versus-answer decision itself is now a first-class research object. ClarifyMT-Bench evaluates 'an LLM's ability to dynamically choose between asking and answering', grounded in a five-dimensional ambiguity taxonomy spanning linguistic, intent, contextual, epistemic, and interactional ambiguity, in contrast to traditional IR methods that treat ambiguity as a static property of the query [14]. AskBench converts standard QA datasets into multi-turn interactions with explicit checkpoints, including an 'AskMind (missing-info clarification)' variant in which the intent is deliberately made deficient [15]. CART targets the complementary failure mode — knowing when not to ask — noting that 'even systems such as OpenAI Deep-Research ask only one clarifying question', so fairly static approaches remain suboptimal for underspecified queries [13].

Evidence that clarification is not uniformly beneficial is also emerging. 'Reasoning About Intent for Ambiguous Requests' compared an Interpretation-Answer Pairs approach, 'which eliminates the need for open-ended clarification, against a traditional Clarification Pipeline', and found that even the best clarification-pipeline configuration underperformed direct interpretation-answering, with failures arising from 'poorly targeted clarification questions, incomplete user simulation, and answer collapse' [16].

sections.title: Domain-specific pipelines: clarification feeding complex query construction
sections.text:
Text-to-SQL has become a major testbed because the clarified intent must be compiled into a precise, executable artifact. An expected-information-gain interactive framework treats 'query interpretation as a collaborative clarification process': it first generates 'a set of plausible SQL candidates using LLM, e.g., GPT-4' and selects clarification questions by expected information gain [18]. AMBISQL first identifies potentially ambiguous phrases and classifies them 'according to our ambiguity taxonomy' before resolving them interactively [17]. DASG embeds 'interactive clarification as a first-class operator within database systems' [19]. BIRD-Interact reimagines text-to-SQL evaluation 'via lens of dynamic interactions', where the LLM tends to 'pose questions aimed at clarifying core concepts' in the initial phase and a user simulator produces clarifications grounded in ground-truth SQL snippets [20]. A multi-turn text-to-SQL benchmark with multiple question types explicitly expects that, for ambiguous questions, 'the system should identify and address this ambiguity by seeking clarification from the user' [21]. User-centered studies of natural-language database interfaces likewise identify mixed-initiative follow-up questions — e.g., 'When you say "sales," do you mean "sales amount" or "number of sales"?' — as a key direction [24].

Related pipelines appear in knowledge-graph question answering, retrieval, infrastructure-as-code, and robotics. CLEAR-KGQA combines 'a Bayesian inference mechanism to quantify query ambiguity' with 'a two-agent interaction framework where an LLM-based user simulator' enables iterative refinement [22]. In retrieval, systems increasingly 'directly generate the next clarification step' with LLMs 'instead of choosing from a pool of candidate questions' [23]. Ambig-IAC generates 'diverse candidate specifications, identifies structural disagreements across the three axes, ranks them by informativeness, and uses the most informative disagreements to generate targeted clarification questions' under a fixed interaction budget [32]. In embodied AI, Ask-to-Clarify learns ambiguity resolution from 'targeted ambiguity-solving interactive dialogue data', where 'the agent engages in a multi-turn dialogue to resolve the ambiguity' of a visual instruction by generating a clarification question at each step [9]; work on ambiguous out-of-view instructions notes that ambiguities can be resolved by 'enabling robots to ask clarifying questions to the user' during action planning [10].

sections.title: Comparative evidence: clarification dialogue versus prompt rewriting
sections.text:
Whether clarification-based prompt composition beats simpler alternatives is still being established. 'Less Back-and-Forth' compares three prompt conditions — a raw prompt, a checklist-improved prompt, and 'a clarifying-question prompt, where the model asked 1-3 questions before producing the final answer' — across summarization, planning, explanation, and coding tasks on ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok. Checklist-improved prompts achieved the highest mean rubric score, 7.50 out of 8, compared with 5.67 for raw prompts and 6.67 for clarifying-question prompts, and produced the best quality-effort tradeoff in tokens [25]. A complementary large-scale study of real human-AI conversations found that 'rephrasing ineffective prompts can elicit better responses from a conversational system, while preserving user intent' [26].

At the framing level, a survey of conversational search positions clarification as 'an inserted dialogue management strategy, seamlessly integrated within the retrieval and generation flow' in RAG-era systems [30], and a survey of LLM knowledge boundaries lists 'asking clarification questions' as a standard alternative to uncertain responses when models meet unknown knowledge [31]. The emerging picture is that clarification Q&A is a well-motivated mechanism for composing better prompts, but its advantage over non-interactive prompt improvement is task- and format-dependent.

sections.title: Synthesis and open gaps
sections.text: Taken together, the answer to the research question is yes, on both halves. Different formats of clarification Q&A are explicitly studied — open-ended [1], yes/no [2], multiple-choice [3][33], and suggestion-style turns offering candidate interpretations [28] — and the clarified intent is routinely fed back as a better-specified prompt for the LLM: a refined task specification [8], an actionable intention [11], a rewritten query [17], or a cost-optimized database query [19]. Three gaps stand out. First, question format itself is rarely ablated in the LLM setting: multiple-choice is compared against open-ended mainly at the level of benchmark design [3], and systematic studies of which format minimizes interaction cost while maximizing prompt fidelity are lacking. Second, the user is often simulated by an LLM-based user simulator [20][22], which complicates transfer to real users. Third, when to ask has become a first-class design axis — clarity prediction [6], Bayesian ambiguity quantification [22], expected-information-gain question selection [18], and explicit cost or budget constraints [19][32] — alongside dedicated benchmarks for the ask-versus-answer decision [13][14][15].

question: Can you recommend a suitable theoretical lens for qualitative research concerning robotics process automation (RPA) implementations?

sections.title: Recommendation: socio-technical systems theory as the primary lens
sections.text: For qualitative research on Robotic Process Automation (RPA) implementations, the most suitable primary theoretical lens is socio-technical systems (STS) theory, which treats an implementation as the product of interacting social and technical factors rather than as a purely technical rollout [2]. STS theory rests on the interdependence of the social and technical aspects of work [1] and has a direct precedent of being applied as a conceptual lens in a case study of process automation adoption [3]. For narrower research questions, well-matched complementary lenses exist: a sociomaterial, practice-based lens for the reconfiguration of work practices [12]; neoinstitutional theory for the legitimacy and isomorphic pressures behind the adoption decision [10]; the technology-organization-environment (TOE) framework for structuring adoption factors [5]; and sociotechnical imaginaries and domestication for longitudinal studies of how automation is envisioned and normalized [11]. Typologies of sociotechnical change theories can be used to position these candidate lenses against each other [14].

sections.title: Why RPA implementation research needs a theoretical lens
sections.text: RPA is an emerging technology automating business processes that combines software, artificial intelligence and machine learning to imitate the activity of human workers, shifting repetitive, rule-based tasks from people to software robots [5]. Because it redistributes work, an implementation is never only a technical event: an exploratory qualitative case study of concrete RPA projects in the automotive industry identified challenges such as understanding the factors influencing user acceptance, explaining RPA to employees, and designing human-bot interaction [8]. Early empirical knowledge of RPA is thin, with most prior research relating to case studies and discussion papers [4], and a 2018 interview study with Big 4 firms found that there is still much that firms do not understand about how using RPA will influence the profession [4]. The social dimension is not merely rhetorical: quantitative evidence from a Dutch ministry showed that RPA use is negatively related to employee autonomy and task variety [13]. For this reason, process automation researchers have argued that the phenomenon is technologically discussed so far and that a holistic social-technical perspective is needed to broaden the view [3]. A theoretical lens is also valuable for the implementation itself, since using a theoretical framework is argued to improve the performance in the implementation of RPA projects and the benefits in automation and process metrics [15]. In qualitative research, theories operate as a lens through which to view the phenomena of interest [7], and the methodological literature recommends making explicit which framework is drawn on and how it is applied [6].

sections.title: What STS theory actually says
sections.text: STS theory is founded on two main principles. First, the interaction of social and technical factors creates the conditions for successful or unsuccessful system performance, comprising partly linear, designed cause-and-effect relationships and partly non-linear, complex, even unpredictable relationships. Second, optimization of either socio, or far more commonly the technical, tends to increase the quantity of unpredictable, non-designed, non-linear relationships that are actually injurious to the system's performance; sociotechnical theory is therefore all about joint optimisation [2]. The theory provides methods of joint optimization for designing organizations that exhibit open systems properties and can thus cope better with environmental complexity, dynamism, new technology, and competition [2]. Its classic formulation, introduced by Trist and Bamforth in 1951, acknowledges the interdependence of the social and technical aspects of work, which collectively form a sociotechnical system [1]. A key implication for implementation research is that design is systemic: altering one part of the system, such as implementing automation technologies, can lead to changes in other parts [1]. STS also distinguishes two stances for studying organizational change: a reactive approach that examines the impacts generated by technological change after implementation, and a proactive approach that anticipates results and prepares the system's maturity beforehand to increase the chances of success [1].

snippets: Sociotechnical refers to the interrelatedness of 'social' and 'technical'. Sociotechnical 'theory' is founded on two main principles. One is that the interaction of social and technical factors creates the conditions for successful (or unsuccessful) system performance.

The corollary of this, and the second of the two main principles, is that optimisation of either socio, or far more commonly the technical, tends to increase not only the quantity of unpredictable, 'un-designed', non-linear relationships, but those relationships that are actually injurious to the system's performance. Sociotechnical 'theory', therefore, is all about 'joint optimisation'.

Sociotechnical systems theory, the term used throughout the current article (and seemingly the term in most widespread use at the present time) reflects certain specific methods of joint optimisation in order to design organisations that exhibit open systems properties and can thus cope better with environmental complexity, dynamism, new technology and competition.

sections.title: Evidence that STS fits qualitative RPA implementation research
sections.text: There is direct precedent for using STS as the theoretical lens of a qualitative automation study. In a revelatory case study of process automation, the authors state: 'We apply the socio-technical system (STS) theory as conceptual lens for our case study in order to broaden the view towards a holistic social-technical perspective on a phenomenon that is technologically discussed so far,' and, drawing on the case results together with STS theory, they present requirements for the adoption of process automation [3]. Marcon et al. applied sociotechnical theory to digital technology implementation in manufacturing with an explicitly qualitative design: a qualitative approach including cross-case and ethnographic analyses across 28 companies, using interviews, plant visits, and longitudinal case studies [1]. Based on sociotechnical theory, the study uses qualitative data to describe how companies established key enabling factors and the interrelationships between different sociotechnical factors, examining the organizational system needed to integrate people, technology, organizational structure, and the overall business environment [1]. Their central warning transfers directly to RPA: companies that solely focus on technical aspects risk encountering challenges related to adoption, integration, and support from stakeholders, ultimately hindering their digital transformation efforts [1]. RPA-specific qualitative evidence shows the social side of implementation is rich: semi-structured interviews with 14 accounting professionals including RPA leaders at the Big 4 firms revealed that bot implementation changed work, increased job satisfaction and career mobility, and reduced offshoring without necessarily reducing headcount [4]. In RPA-enabled collaborative networks 4.0, the sociotechnical achievements include worker inclusion - workers adapting to RPA configuration and operation needs, including training and moving to new functions - and user satisfaction with new and integrated services [9]. Finally, a manufacturing study argues that using the proposed theoretical framework and approaches can improve the performance in the implementation of RPA and intelligent process automation projects and increase the benefits in automation and process metrics [15].

sections.title: How the STS lens shapes qualitative method design
sections.text: A theoretical lens shapes qualitative design in four steps. First, researchers should articulate which theoretical framework they are drawing on and how it will be applied, reflecting on the purpose and the context of the study [6]. Second, the choice is not a declaration of pure inductivism: it is hard to be convinced that a study can be wholly inductive, since all knowledge is theory-laden and researchers draw on antecedent research to form a research question and to guide the research design [6]. Third, orienting concepts from a predetermined theory should be used to sensitize the researcher to the phenomenon, advocate the research question and objectives, guide the research design, illuminate data collection, and assist with data analysis and interpretation [6]. Fourth, because theories operate as a lens through which to view the phenomena of interest, the lens choice should be defensible with respect to the phenomenon under study [7]. STS's core idea of joint optimization translates into a concrete sampling rule for RPA implementation research: collect qualitative data from both subsystems - not only process owners and IT specialists but also affected employees, managers, and vendors - and attend to the interactions between elements rather than to their individual characteristics [2][1]. A published qualitative implementation study illustrates the design in practice: a qualitative approach with multiple interviews, plant visits, longitudinal case studies, and cross-case and ethnographic analysis, following established multi-interview case method guidance [1]. The reactive/proactive distinction in STS can additionally structure the analysis of how organizations learn from earlier automation attempts and prepare for new ones [1].

sections.title: Complementary and alternative lenses
sections.text: If the research question is narrower, a different lens may fit better. For questions about how day-to-day work practices are reconfigured around software robots, a sociomaterial, practice-based lens is suitable: practice-based research has a dedicated methodological literature, and its standard account for studying technology in organizations is Orlikowski's practice lens, 'Using Technology and Constituting Structures' [12]. For questions about why organizations adopt RPA in the first place - mimetic, coercive, or normative pressures - a neoinstitutional theoretical lens offers the concept of isomorphic processes; although its use has been dominated by sociologists of organizational behavior, it is increasingly employed by researchers in management science and information systems to explain the phenomenon of new technologies adoption by businesses [10]. For questions about the factor structure of adoption decisions, the TOE framework organizes antecedents into technological, organizational, and environmental contexts; a study of RPA adoption during the pandemic explicitly recommends proposing and testing a framework from the TOE theory to explain SMEs' adoption of the RPA technology [5]. For longitudinal, cultural questions about how automation is envisioned, adopted, and normalized over time, sociotechnical imaginaries and domestication provide a conceptual lens, since the impact of new technologies is shaped not only by technical features but also by how people envision, adopt, and normalize them in practice [11]. A typology of sociotechnical change theories lists these candidate lenses - sociotechnical transitions, social practice theory, discourse theory, domestication theory, large technical systems, social construction of technology, sociotechnical imaginaries, actor-network theory - so that a researcher's choice can be positioned and defended [14].

sections.title: Practical decision rule and caveats
sections.text: A practical decision rule: choose STS theory when the question concerns how an RPA implementation unfolds - how technical and social elements are jointly reconfigured and how benefits or failures emerge from their interaction [1][2]. Choose the practice/sociomaterial lens when the unit of analysis is the reconfiguration of work practices around bots [12]; neoinstitutional theory when the adoption decision and its legitimacy are the object of study [10]; TOE when the goal is a structured inventory of adoption factors across technological, organizational, and environmental contexts [5]; and sociotechnical imaginaries/domestication when the interest is in long-term normalization of automation [11]. Whichever lens is chosen, avoid the two classic failure modes identified in the methodological literature: under-use of theory, which leaves the study with purely descriptive information rather than an interpretation explaining the why and how, and over-reliance on a theory, which can reduce the development of new knowledge that is critically important to the progress of a field [6]. A balanced design applies the lens consistently across research design, data collection, and analysis while remaining open to data that challenge the theory's initial assumptions [6].

question: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees in terms of computation complexity.

sections.title: Introduction: Two Families of Tree Compression and Their Cost Axes
sections.text: Algorithms for compressing trees divide into two families, and the families differ on every complexity axis at once. The first is repetition- or grammar-based compression, in which a tree is replaced by a smaller representation — a directed acyclic graph (dag), a tree grammar, or a straight-line program — that shares repeated substructures, with the general goal of developing "algorithms that directly work on compressed data without prior decompression" [1]. Bille et al. organize the existing schemes into "three major approaches: using subtree repeats, using tree pattern repeats, and using succinct data structures" [2], and their top-tree scheme is designed to combine the strongest properties of each: it "achieves close to optimal worst-case compression, can compress exponentially better than DAG compression, is never much worse than DAG compression, and supports navigational queries in logarithmic time" [2]. The second family, succinct representation, aims for encodings that "use space that is close to the appropriate information-theoretic minimum, but support operations on the tree rapidly, usually in O(1) time" [4]. Because the two families optimize different objectives, any comparison of computational complexity must track three quantities: the time to build the compressed representation, the size of that representation (compression ratio or bit count), and the time to answer queries directly on the compressed form, without decompressing. The sections below compare the representative algorithms along these axes.

Our compression scheme is the first to simultaneously take advantage of internal repeats in the tree (as opposed to the classical DAG compression that only exploits rooted subtree repeats) while also supporting fast navigational queries directly on the compressed representation.

We show that the new compression scheme achieves close to optimal worst-case compression, can compress exponentially better than DAG compression, is never much worse than DAG compression, and supports navigational queries in logarithmic time.

Over all possible DAGs that can represent $T$ , the smallest one is unique and can be computed in $O(n)$ time [12]. Its size can be exponentially smaller than $n$ .

Unfortunately, computing a minimal tree grammar is NP-Hard [10], and all known tree grammar based compression schemes can only support navigational queries in time proportional to the height of the grammar which can be $\Omega(n)$ .
Note that with standard DAG compression the worst-case bound is $\Theta(n_T)$ since a single path is incompressible using subtree repeats.

Theorem 1 Let $T$ be any ordered tree with nodes labeled from an alphabet of size $\sigma$ and let $\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}$ be the corresponding top DAG. Then, $n_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}} = O(n_T / \log_{\sigma}^{0.19}n_T)$ .
Thus, top DAG compression can be exponentially better than DAG compression (since it's possible that $n_D = O(\log n_T)$ ) and it is always within a logarithmic factor of DAG compression.

Theorem 3 Let $T$ be an ordered tree with top DAG $\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}$ . There is an $O(n_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}})$ space representation of $T$ that supports Access, Depth, Height, Size, Parent, Firstchild, NextSibling, LevelAncestor, and NCA in $O(\log n_T)$ time. Furthermore, we can Decompress a subtree $T'$ of $T$ in time $O(\log n_T + |T'|)$ .

For labeled trees, Ferragina et al. [13] gave a representation using $2n\log \sigma + O(n)$ bits that supports basic navigational operations, such as find the parent of node $v$ , the $i$'th child of $v$ , and any child of $v$ with label $\alpha$ .
Note that the above space bounds do not guarantee a compact representation when the input contains many subtree repeats or tree pattern repeats. In particular, the total space is never $o(n)$ bits.

Jacobson [17] was the first to observe that the naive pointer-based tree representation using $\Theta(n\log n)$ bits is wasteful. He showed that unlabeled trees can be represented using $2n + o(n)$ bits and support various queries by inspection of $\Theta(\lg n)$ bits in the bit probe model. This space bound is asymptotically optimal with the information-theoretic lower bound. Munro and Raman [26] showed how to achieve the same bound in the RAM model while using only constant time for queries.

sections.title: DAG (Subtree-Sharing) Compression: Linear-Time Construction, Logarithmic Navigation, PSPACE-Hard General Queries
sections.text: DAG compression replaces every repeated rooted subtree by a single shared node, and it is the cheapest family to build: of all dags that can represent a given tree, "the smallest one is unique and can be computed in O(n) time," and its size "can be exponentially smaller than n" [2]. The limitation is that sharing is restricted to whole rooted subtrees: a dag of size m can only encode trees whose size is "bounded exponentially in" m, so in the theoretical optimum dags allow merely "singly exponential compression rates" [1], and in the worst case there is no compression at all, since "with standard DAG compression the worst-case bound is Θ(n_T) since a single path is incompressible using subtree repeats" [2]. Navigation on the compressed dag is fast — Bille et al. note that navigational and path queries can be answered directly on the DAG representation in logarithmic time [2] — but general algorithmic problems on dag-compressed trees become hard: core XPath evaluation over dag-compressed trees is PSPACE-complete, a result Lohrey and Maneth then extend "to linear SL cf tree grammars (Theorem 9)" [1], and their Table 1 places membership for deterministic top-down tree automata on dags at NL-complete and bottom-up membership at P-complete, with bounds across the considered representation classes ranging from NL (nondeterministic logspace) to PSPACE (polynomial space) [1]. In practice the per-step cost of building such sharing structures is modest: for state compression in model checking, the time complexity, "measured in the number of hash table accesses, is linear in the number of state slots" [6], the scheme can "compress even large states to a small constant on average (8 bytes)" [6], and the median measured compression ratio is within 17% of the optimum for tree compression [6].

snippets: Whereas a dag can be seen as a regular tree grammar [7] that generates exactly one tree, an SL cf tree grammar is a context-free tree grammar [7] that generates exactly one tree. SL cf tree grammars allow to share identical intermediate parts in a tree. This results in better compression rates in comparison to dags: in the theoretical optimum, SL cf tree grammars lead to doubly exponential compression rates, whereas dags only allow singly exponential compression rates.

In [11] it was shown that the evaluation problem for core XPath (the navigational part of XPath) over dag-compressed trees is PSPACE-complete. Here, we extend this result to linear SL cf tree grammars (Theorem 9). This is remarkable, since linear SL cf tree grammars lead to (provably) better compression rates than dags.
For all cases, we present upper and lower bounds which vary from NL (nondeterministic logspace) to PSPACE (polynomial space). Our results are collected in Table 1.

sections.title: Grammar-Based and SLP Compression: Deeper Compression, Intractable Optimization, Degraded Query Time
sections.text: Tree grammars — equivalently, straight-line context-free tree grammars or straight-line programs — generalize dags: their productions "allow to share identical intermediate parts in a tree," not just entire subtrees. The payoff in compression is the largest of any scheme studied: "in the theoretical optimum, SL cf tree grammars lead to doubly exponential compression rates, whereas dags only allow singly exponential compression rates" [1]. The practical BPLEX algorithm generates a small SL cf tree grammar for a given input tree, and experiments on existing XML benchmark data show that it "results in significantly better compression rates than dag-based compression algorithms" [1]. The price is paid on both sides of the complexity ledger. First, compression is hard to optimize: "computing a minimal tree grammar is NP-Hard" [2], and for ordered rooted trees compressed by variable-replacement grammars, "there is no polynomial time algorithm with approximation ratio less than 8593/8592 unless P = NP" [3] — a stronger negative result than plain NP-hardness, since even constant-factor approximation is ruled out. This is why the deployed algorithm is greedy: it "is based on a greedy approach of replacing isomorphic subtrees" and replaces them "by the same variable in order of increasing the size" of the replaced subtree [3]. That greedy algorithm is nonetheless polynomial: its preprocessing step runs "in O(|V_U|+A^2 N+A|F'_{U,r}||A|) time" and the main loop "in O(B M C) time" [3], so the whole construction finishes "in O(|V_U| + A^2 N + A|F'_{U,r}||Λ| + BMC) time," where the parameters bound the sizes and occurrence counts of the candidate (pseudo-)patterns and C counts the variables of the output grammar [3]. Second, operations on the compressed form degrade: "all known tree grammar based compression schemes can only support navigational queries in time proportional to the height of the grammar which can be Ω(n)" [2], and XPath evaluation stays PSPACE-complete even when the grammar is restricted to be linear, since the PSPACE-completeness result for dags extends "to linear SL cf tree grammars (Theorem 9)" [1].

sections.title: Top Tree Compression: Pattern Repeats with Logarithmic Query Time
sections.text: Top tree compression targets the weakness of the two earlier families — dags miss internal repeats, while tree grammars make navigation take time proportional to the grammar height, i.e. Ω(n) [2] — by first transforming the input tree with a top-tree decomposition "such that tree pattern repeats in T become subtree repeats," and then applying classical DAG compression to the transformed tree. The worst-case guarantee is the strongest among repetition-based schemes: the resulting top DAG satisfies "n_TD = O(n_T / log_σ^0.19 n_T)" (Theorem 1), close to the information-theoretic bound of Ω(n_T / log_σ n_T) [2]. Relative to plain DAG compression, top tree compression "can compress exponentially better than DAG compression," and "it is always within a logarithmic factor of DAG compression" (Theorem 2) [2]. Querying costs a logarithm: there is an O(n_TD)-space representation of the tree that "supports Access, Depth, Height, Size, Parent, Firstchild, NextSibling, LevelAncestor, and NCA in O(log n_T) time," and "we can Decompress a subtree T' of T in time O(log n_T + |T'|)" (Theorem 3) [2]. In short, the scheme buys the deep compression of tree grammars while retaining dag-like logarithmic query complexity, at the price of an extra logarithmic factor compared to the O(1) queries of succinct encodings.

snippets: The key idea in top tree compression is to transform the input tree $T$ into another tree $\mathcal{T}$ such that tree pattern repeats in $T$ become subtree repeats in $\mathcal{T}$ . The transformation is based on top trees [2-4] - a data structure originally designed for dynamic (uncompressed) trees.

Theorem 1 Let $T$ be any ordered tree with nodes labeled from an alphabet of size $\sigma$ and let $\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}$ be the corresponding top DAG. Then, $n_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}} = O(n_T / \log_{\sigma}^{0.19}n_T)$ .
This worst-case performance of the top DAG should be compared to the information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(n_T / \log_\sigma n_T)$ .
we show that top tree compression (iv) can compress exponentially better than DAG compression, and (v) is never worse than DAG compression by more than a log $n$ factor.
Thus, top DAG compression can be exponentially better than DAG compression (since it's possible that $n_D = O(\log n_T)$ ) and it is always within a logarithmic factor of DAG compression.

Theorem 3 Let $T$ be an ordered tree with top DAG $\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}$ . There is an $O(n_{\mathcal{T}\mathcal{D}})$ space representation of $T$ that supports Access, Depth, Height, Size, Parent, Firstchild, NextSibling, LevelAncestor, and NCA in $O(\log n_T)$ time. Furthermore, we can Decompress a subtree $T'$ of $T$ in time $O(\log n_T + |T'|)$ .

sections.title: Succinct Representations: Information-Theoretic Space with Constant-Time Queries
sections.text: The succinct family optimizes space to the information-theoretic limit rather than exploiting repeats. Since there are only C_{n-1} = (1/n)·binom(2n-2, n-1) ordinal trees on n nodes, "there is an information-theoretic worst-case lower bound of lg C_{n-1} = 2n − O(lg n) bits on any ordinal tree representation" [4]. The canonical construction is Jacobson's LOUDS encoding, which "uses 2n + O(1) bits to encode an ordinal tree on n nodes, and an additional o(n) bits to support rank and select operations"; Jacobson supported these operations "in O(lg n) probes" in the bit-probe model, and "Clark and Munro further showed how to support the rank and select operations in O(1) time under the word RAM model," yielding constant-time parent, child, and child_rank operations [4]. A parallel construction, the balanced-parenthesis representation of Munro and Raman, gives "a succinct representation of an ordinal tree on n nodes in 2n + o(n) bits based on BP, which supports parent, desc, depth" and the rank/select operations "in constant time, and child (x,i) in O(i) time" [4]; in general, "a number of succinct representations have been developed that use only 2n + o(n) bits of space, and support a wide variety of navigational and other operations in O(1) time on the word RAM model" [4]. Labeled trees cost more: "a representation using 2n log σ + O(n) bits" supports basic navigational operations, and under a Markov-like model in which a node's label is a function of its ancestors, "at most nH_k(T) + 2.01n + o(n) bits" suffice [2]. The structural contrast with the repetition-based family is absolute: "the total space is never o(n) bits," so succinct encodings cannot exploit repeated substructure at all [2]. The same near-optimal building blocks are reused in the grammar-compressed-index literature, where the tree structures attached to grammar symbols are stored in encodings such as DFUDS, for which "Most take 2N + o(N) bits of space" and which "answers in constant time" the standard navigational operations [7].

snippets: As there are $C_{n-1} = \frac{1}{n}\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$ ordinal trees on $n$ nodes, there is an information-theoretic worst-case lower bound of $\lg C_{n-1} = 2n - O(\lg n)$ bits on any ordinal tree representation, and there is a trivial encoding of an $n$ -node ordinal tree as an integer of $\lceil \lg C_{n-1} \rceil$ bits.

Jacobson [26] proposed the first succinct tree representation for ordinal trees. His representation is based on the level order unary degree sequence (LOUDS) of a tree, which visits the nodes in a level-order traversal of the tree and encodes their degrees in unary.

This representation uses $2n + O(1)$ bits to encode an ordinal tree on $n$ nodes, and an additional $o(n)$ bits to support rank and select operations on the encoding. Jacobson considered these operations in the bit probe model, and showed how to support them in $O(\lg n)$ probes. Clark and Munro [10] further showed how to support the rank and select operations in $O(1)$ time under the word RAM model with $\Theta(\lg n)$ word size. Thus the LOUDS representation supports parent, child and child_rank operations in $O(1)$ time.

On the other hand, as we will see, a number of succinct representations have been developed that use only $2n + o(n)$ bits of space, and support a wide variety of navigational and other operations in $O(1)$ time on the word RAM model.

Munro and Raman [33] presented a succinct representation of an ordinal tree on $n$ nodes in $2n + o(n)$ bits based on BP, which supports parent, desc, depth, $\mathrm{rank}_{\mathrm{PRE / POST}}$ and $\mathrm{select}_{\mathrm{PRE / POST}}$ in constant time, and child $(x,i)$ in $O(i)$ time.

sections.title: Key Compression for In-Memory Search Trees: The Encoding-Speed Dimension
sections.text: A final, systems-oriented variant compresses not the tree structure but the string keys stored in an in-memory search tree, under the extra constraint that the encoding preserve order so that range queries still work. Here the relevant complexity axis is per-key encoding speed rather than worst-case space: the six schemes evaluated "make different trade-offs between compression rate and encoding speed" [5]. Generic block compressors are excluded on complexity grounds: "for in-memory search trees, however, block compression algorithms impose too much computational overhead because the DBMS is unable to operate directly on the search tree data without having to decompress it first," since "query latencies for in-memory B+trees and tries range from 100s of nanoseconds to a few microseconds, while the fastest block compression algorithms can decompress only a few 4 KB memory pages in that time" [5]. HOPE therefore adopts "emphasis on encoding speed (rather than decoding) because our target search tree queries need not reconstruct the original keys," encoding with fixed-length codes or optimal order-preserving prefix codes [5]. The result is that the instrumented search trees achieve "lower query latency (up to 40% lower) and better memory efficiency (up to 30% smaller) simultaneously for most string key workloads" [5] — evidence that on this axis, a cheaper encoder on which the data structure can operate directly beats a slower, more heavily compressing one.

snippets: We then select six representative compression schemes using this model and implement them in HOPE. These schemes make different trade-offs between compression rate and encoding speed.

Block compression algorithms, however, are too slow for in-memory search trees: query latencies for in-memory B+trees and tries range from 100s of nanoseconds to a few microseconds, while the fastest block compression algorithms can decompress only a few 4 KB memory pages in that time [7].
A key insight in HOPE is its emphasis on encoding speed (rather than decoding) because our target search tree queries need not reconstruct the original keys.

Our experiments show that using HOPE allows the search trees to achieve lower query latency (up to $40\%$ lower) and better memory efficiency (up to $30\%$ smaller) simultaneously for most string key workloads.

sections.title: Summary of the Complexity Trade-offs
sections.text: Comparing the algorithms along the three axes gives a consistent picture. DAG compression is O(n) to build [2], achieves at most singly exponential compression [1], is Θ(n) in the worst case [2], supports navigational queries in logarithmic time [2], but makes XPath evaluation PSPACE-complete [1]. Tree-grammar/SLP compression reaches doubly exponential rates in the theoretical optimum [1], and BPLEX beats DAG compression in practice [1], but the optimum is NP-hard to compute [2] and hard even to approximate within a small constant [3]; the best known greedy construction is polynomial, running in O(|V_U| + A^2 N + A|F'_{U,r}||Λ| + BMC) time [3]; navigation costs Ω(n) in the worst case [2]; and XPath remains PSPACE-complete even for linear grammars [1]. Top tree compression interpolates between the two, with a worst-case compression ratio of at least log_σ^0.19 n and O(log n)-time queries on an O(n_TD)-space representation [2]. Succinct encodings sit at the opposite end: 2n + o(n) bits, asymptotically optimal [4], with O(1) query time [4], but they never use o(n) space, so they cannot exploit repeats at all [2]. Key-level order-preserving compression replaces the space/time trade-off with a per-key compression-rate-versus-encoding-speed trade-off [5]. The residual tension is stated explicitly by work on universal tree source codes: "for very compressible trees, the space savings in hypersuccinct trees are no longer competitive," while "constant-time queries are not possible in the regime of mildly compressible strings; the same applies to known approaches to represent trees" [8]. In short: repetition-based schemes buy exponential compression at the price of PSPACE-hard general queries or Ω(n) navigation, while succinct schemes buy constant-time queries at the price of linear space — and no single published scheme dominates on all three axes.

question: Describe what is known about overfitting in in-context learning.

sections.title: Overfitting in In-Context Learning: Framing the Problem
sections.text: In-context learning (ICL) is the ability of a trained model to perform a task from input-output demonstrations supplied in the input prompt; it happens "only at inference time without any parameter updates to the model" [1]. Because no weights change during inference, "overfitting" is studied in ICL in several distinct senses. First, during pretraining, the model may fail to acquire a general task-learning algorithm and instead memorize the specific tasks it was trained on, so its in-context behavior overfits to the pretraining task distribution; Garg et al. already noted that "it is unclear to what extent these models have developed the ability to learn new tasks from in-context examples alone as opposed to simply indexing into a vast set of known tasks from the training data" [1]. Second, at test time, the model's prediction can overfit to the particular in-context demonstrations — their labels, format, and surface statistics — rather than to the underlying task mapping [13][14]. Third, in iterative test-time refinement pipelines, using the model's own high-confidence outputs as pseudo-labeled demonstrations can cause the system to "reinforce biases present in these data," ultimately degrading performance [3]. A further complication is that some gains attributed to ICL may actually come from the model surfacing memorized pretraining data rather than generalizing from the demonstrations [2].

sections.title: Benign Overfitting In-Context: Memorizing Noisy Demonstrations Yet Generalizing
sections.text: Frei and Vardi analyzed linear transformers trained by gradient descent on random linear classification tasks and characterized, via an analysis of the implicit regularization of gradient descent, "how many pre-training tasks and in-context examples are needed for the trained transformer to generalize well at test-time" [4]. They found that "after pre-training the transformer can tolerate smaller SNR than those tasks which it was trained on" and that "at test time the transformer can tolerate label-flipping noise, even though the pre-training data does not have label-flipping noise" [4]. Their central overfitting result is what they call "benign overfitting in-context": "when in-context examples are corrupted by label flipping noise, the transformer memorizes all of its in-context examples (including those with noisy labels) yet still generalizes near-optimally for clean test examples" [4]. This regime requires "the features to lie in a high-dimensional space and for the SNR to be relatively small" [4]. Mechanistically, they show that "the forward pass of a pre-trained transformer behaves similarly to an average over the in-context training examples," and use this averaging behavior to prove the benign-overfitting guarantee [4]. To their knowledge, no prior work had demonstrated that transformers could exhibit benign overfitting [4]. The practical takeaway is that exactly memorizing (noisy) demonstrations is not inherently harmful: a model can interpolate the in-context examples perfectly and still be near-optimal on new test inputs.

snippets: In this work, we investigate the behavior of linear transformers trained on random linear classification tasks. Via an analysis of the implicit regularization of gradient descent, we characterize how many pre-training tasks and in-context examples are needed for the trained transformer to generalize well at test-time.

sections.title: Overfitting to the Pretraining Task Distribution: Distribution Shift and Transient Abilities
sections.text: A complementary line of work probes whether trained models overfit the exact prompt distribution they were trained on. Garg et al. trained transformers on prompts whose in-context example outputs contained no noise, then tested under "two forms of distribution shift: (i) between the training data of the model and inference-time prompts, and (ii) between the in-context examples and the query input during inference" [1]. They found that "the performance of our model is quite robust to such shifts, indicating that it has learned to perform linear regression with some generality," and that "increasing the capacity often significantly improves performance with distribution shifts, even when the absolute improvement in the standard error is small" [1]. More recent theory quantifies when shift does hurt: Demir and Dogan derive closed-form generalization-error expressions for ICL on linear regression tasks and "prove that shifts in input covariance or label noise substantially impair ICL, but that an optimal attention temperature exists which minimizes this error" [5]. Overfitting can also occur during pretraining itself: training-dynamics studies report that "ICL may often be a transient ability that the transformers acquire and then lose over the course of long training time, a phenomenon that has since been reproduced in many settings" [6], consistent with the weights overfitting to the particular structure of the training tasks rather than settling on a stable task-learning algorithm.

sections.title: Overfitting by Over-Exposure: The Many-Shot Regime
sections.text: With long-context models, the number of demonstrations can be increased from a handful to thousands. Rather than improving monotonically, ICL accuracy typically plateaus and then declines. Baek et al. observed "that while performance generally improves as the number of in-context examples increases, it eventually plateaus and begins to decline as the context length approaches the limit," a diminishing return that "highlights the need to carefully balance context length and example quantity" [7]. They further found that long-context models "exhibit robustness to noisy examples in relatively simple tasks, but become vulnerable to noise in more complex scenarios to which they might be less exposed during training, such as extremely low-resource translation tasks" [7]. Zhang et al. attribute the many-shot degradation to "the suboptimal negative log-likelihood (NLL) optimization objective and the incremental data noise," reporting that "as the number of ICL examples increases, models' performance exhibits a trend of rising and then falling" [8]. Hu et al. conclude that "LLMs are effective few-shot learners but not many-shot learners," since they "struggle in many-shot settings due to the challenges of long-context integration" [9]. On academic knowledge benchmarks, Honda et al. observed "no performance improvement when increasing the number of in-context demonstrations from few-shot to many-shot," and note that "the essence of many-shot learning lies not in the number of examples, but in the number of tokens in context" [10]. FewMMBench similarly found "no consistent gains from increasing the number of demonstrations" between 4-shot and 8-shot support sets, with "accuracy even declin[ing] with more examples" in several cases, attributed to "context dilution, where additional demonstrations introduce noise or distract from task-relevant information" [11]. In dynamic grid-world tasks, Ye et al. report that ICL "is not uniformly advantageous and can even underperform zero-shot" and that "models sometimes overfit to the provided examples and underweight the actual attributes of the current scene" [12].

sections.title: Overfitting to Surface Form: Label Fixation and Format-Driven Shortcuts
sections.text: A further mode of overfitting is to the surface statistics of demonstrations rather than their semantic mapping. Liu shows that "homogeneous labels—even semantically valid ones—collapse accuracy to ≤ 12% across six models (Pythia, Llama, Qwen; 0.8B-8B) and four tasks," because "the model treats tokens occupying the label position as an exhaustive answer vocabulary, with homogeneity as the maximally collapsed case" [13]. This behavior "is inconsistent with latent-concept Bayesian accounts" and "reveals that ICL output is constrained vocabulary retrieval—the model binds its output to the demonstrated token inventory regardless of semantic plausibility" [13]. Although many-shot ICL has been shown to overcome some ICL biases, "whether fixation yields to many-shot regimes is an open question," since 16-shot experiments on Pythia-1B showed the collapse persisting [13]. In multimodal models, large multimodal models "tend to rely on the distribution of ICDs to narrow the prediction space, e.g., in Visual Question Answering (VQA), a LMM might recognize the ICD answer format and respond an answer in the same format, rather than learning the correct function as in language QA" [14], and overly similar demonstrations "can lead LMMs to copy captions through shortcut inference, rather than generalizing to new examples" [14]. These findings coexist with evidence that models do use label content: a closer look at input-label demonstrations found "a considerable relationship between the performance and label correctness" [15].

sections.title: Memorization of Pretraining Data as a Hidden Driver of ICL Performance
sections.text: Finally, some of the behavior attributed to in-context learning may be overfitting to the pretraining corpus itself: the demonstrations act as retrieval cues for memorized training instances rather than as task supervision. Golchin et al. were "the first to show how ICL surfaces memorized training data," and report that "ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases" and that "demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization" [2]. They also find that "there is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL when it outperforms zero-shot learning" [2]. Their study "uncovers memorization as a new factor impacting ICL, raising an important question: to what extent do LLMs truly generalize from demonstrations in ICL, and how much of their success is due to memorization?" [2].

snippets: This study is the first to show how ICL surfaces memorized training data and to explore the correlation between this memorization and performance on downstream tasks across various ICL regimes: zero-shot, few-shot, and many-shot.

Our most notable findings include: (1) ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases; (2) demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization; (3) ICL improves performance when the surfaced memorization in few-shot regimes reaches a high level (about 40%); and (4) there is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL when it outperforms zero-shot learning.

Overall, our study uncovers memorization as a new factor impacting ICL, raising an important question: to what extent do LLMs truly generalize from demonstrations in ICL, and how much of their success is due to memorization?

sections.title: Mitigations and Open Problems
sections.text: Several mitigations for the overfitting-like failures above have been proposed. For shift-induced degradation, choosing the attention temperature to match the distribution shift can recover or even surpass baseline ICL performance, establishing temperature "as a principled and powerful mechanism for improving the robustness of ICL in pretrained Transformers" [5]. For many-shot noise, reweighting demonstrations by their loss (advantage-based reweighting) reduces the impact of noisy examples [8], and distilling many-shot knowledge into a compact "cheat sheet" summary can match many-shot ICL with far fewer tokens, reducing exposure to demonstration noise [10]. For under-utilized context windows, a simple data augmentation approach "substantially improve[s] ICL performance by 5%" when available examples do not fill the window [7]. For shift-tolerance more generally, increasing model capacity improves performance under distribution shift [1]. Open questions remain: under exactly which conditions in-context overfitting is benign rather than harmful [4]; how much of ICL performance is genuine generalization versus retrieval of memorized pretraining data [2]; whether fixation on the demonstrated label inventory can be overcome in many-shot regimes [13]; and why the ICL ability can be a transient one during long training runs [6].
