question: Does active learning work well when fine-tuning large language models?

sections.title: What active learning is, and why it matters for fine-tuning
sections.text: Active learning is a framework for reducing annotation cost: under a budget constraint on how many unlabeled instances can be queried, the learner selectively labels the most informative examples, and it is well established that a model can often reach performance similar to the full-data case using only a small fraction of the available observations [1]. The classical query strategies are uncertainty-based (select what the model is least confident about), diversity-based (cover the input space), and hybrids [1]. These ideas carry directly into fine-tuning pre-trained models: even the adaptation stages of a large language model can demand significant annotated data, and naive fine-tuning under data scarcity risks overfitting, catastrophic forgetting, and poor generalization, so selecting informative examples with uncertainty or diversity criteria is a standard remedy [3]. In the LLM era the picture broadens: large language models are no longer only the models being adapted — they are used inside the active learning loop itself as selectors, synthetic-data generators, and low-cost annotators [2]. LLM-based selection or generation can also reduce training costs such as for supervised fine-tuning, in contrast to the main focus of traditional active learning on reducing labeling costs [2].

snippets: Active learning can be used to select a subset of the data for labeling in order to improve the performance of the model, when there is a budget constraint on the number of unlabeled observations that can be queried.

Indeed, there are many examples of how a classification or regression model can achieve a performance that is similar to what can be achieved when all the labels are available, using only a small fraction of the available observations.

sections.title: Active fine-tuning of pre-trained language models: real gains, mixed evidence
sections.text: Before the scale of today's LLMs, active fine-tuning was studied on pre-trained encoder models, where the fine-tuning stage remained demanding in labeled data [4]. AcTune couples active annotation with self-training for such fine-tuning: it queries high-uncertainty samples for annotation and reuses low-uncertainty pseudo-labels for self-training, and in experiments on six text classification datasets it outperforms the strongest active learning and self-training baselines, improving the label efficiency of pre-trained language model fine-tuning by 56.2% on average [4]. Two caveats emerge from the literature. First, raw uncertainty is a poor query signal on its own: directly sampling the most uncertain instances tends to query repetitive data that represents the overall distribution poorly, which is why AcTune adds region-aware, diversity-promoting sampling [4]. Second, the broader evidence for active learning with transformer fine-tuning is mixed: among the first studies, active learning enhanced BERT classifiers particularly in low-data scenarios, but most subsequent works report mixed results, with improvements that are modest compared to older NLP models [5]. So for fine-tuning pre-trained language models, active learning delivers real label-efficiency gains, but mainly in data-scarce regimes and when uncertainty is combined with diversity.

sections.title: Few-shot and downstream fine-tuning in the LLM era: LLM-assisted selection works
sections.text: When the model being fine-tuned is small and the label budget is tiny, classical active learning hits a cold-start problem: with almost no labeled data at the start of annotation, the system cannot accurately measure informativeness and select informative samples [5]. Recent work exploits an external LLM as the query model to fix this. ActiveLLM uses LLMs such as GPT-4, o1, or Llama 3 to select instances without any training during annotation, and it significantly enhances the classification performance of BERT classifiers in few-shot scenarios, outperforming traditional active learning methods as well as the few-shot methods ADAPET, PERFECT, and SetFit, and can even be used to warm-start other active learning strategies so they overcome their cold-start problem [5]. The same label-efficiency logic motivates one-batch active learning and experimental-design variants for supervised fine-tuning of LLMs [14]. In these settings — small target models, small budgets, domain shift — active selection works well.

sections.title: Instruction tuning: quality beats quantity, but simple selection is a strong baseline
sections.text: For instruction tuning of LLMs, the dominant finding is that data quality matters more than quantity: a model fine-tuned on merely 1,000 carefully curated instruction examples can achieve performance comparable, and in some cases superior, to models trained on vastly larger automatically generated datasets (LIMA), and indicator-based selectors such as IFD significantly outperform an Alpaca model using only about 5% of the Alpaca dataset [6]. Automated selection methods report large gains at these scales: the influence-function-based In2Core achieves similar performance with just 50% of the instruction-fine-tuning data while producing a model that outperforms the one trained on the full training set [7], and the D3 coreset method, built on diversity, difficulty, and dependability, achieves competitive or even superior performance to full-dataset fine-tuning with 5–10% of the data [9]. The picture changes, however, when selection is tested at production scale — selecting up to 2.5M samples from pools of up to 5.8M: many recently proposed methods fall short of random selection in this setting (while using more compute), and 4 of the 7 methods examined even decline in performance as the data pool they select over grows [8]. In that regime a simple representation-based method (RDS+, weighted mean pooling of pretrained LM hidden states) consistently outperforms more complex methods across all settings, beats random selection by an average of two points when controlling for the compute used during selection, and even outperforms the human-curated mixture used to train TULU 2 [8]. The practical reading is that for instruction tuning, selection works — but the winner is often a cheap method, and the elaborate selectors studied in small-scale settings do not automatically scale [6][8].

sections.title: Preference optimization: selection helps offline, but random is hard to beat online
sections.text: For preference-based alignment, the evidence splits by setting. In offline DPO, human preference data is costly and inefficient to collect [10]. A variance-based informativeness measure (preference variance, PVar) predicts how much a prompt contributes to DPO updates: an upper bound shows that prompts with low PVar can only produce small gradient updates, making them less valuable for learning, and experimentally prompts with higher PVar outperform randomly selected prompts — training on only the top 10% of highest-PVar prompts from UltraFeedback even yields better evaluation performance than training on the full dataset [10]. Earlier work likewise framed RLHF preference collection as an active-query problem, developing an algorithm (ADPO) that drastically cuts the number of preference queries needed for LLM alignment [2]. In online DPO with modern LLMs, by contrast, a controlled study of uncertainty-based Active Preference Learning (APL) versus random pair selection finds a counter-intuitive negative result: APL offers little to no benefit over random sampling, with negligible improvements in proxy win-rates [11]. The authors attribute this to the strong priors that modern LLMs inherit from web-scale pretraining — which limit the headroom of post-training data-selection strategies — and to the richness of the on-policy candidate pool, since these models often require minimal steering, rendering random sampling a formidable baseline that offers cheap diversity at near-zero selection cost [11]. They also warn that proxy win-rate can improve even as general capability degrades, so apparent selection gains should be sanity-checked against standard benchmarks [11].

sections.title: RL fine-tuning of reasoning models: online active selection works
sections.text: The clearest positive regime for active selection in LLM fine-tuning is RL-based post-training of reasoning models, where the informativeness of each prompt changes over the course of training. RL finetuning of large language models has become a key technique for enhancing reasoning abilities, but its effectiveness critically depends on the selection of training data [12]. When the model consistently answers a problem either correctly or incorrectly, the reward provides limited optimization signals, and for algorithms such as GRPO the normalized advantages vanish, effectively halting optimization [12]. Online prompt selection that keeps only partially solved prompts is therefore a standard, effective technique — for example, Dynamic Sampling expands candidate batches, discards prompts with consistent rewards, and significantly accelerates RL finetuning in training steps, at the cost of expensive rollouts [12]. Active, dynamics-aware selection works well in this regime: Dynamics-Predictive Sampling models each prompt's solving progress as a hidden Markov process and uses online Bayesian inference to select informative prompts before costly rollouts; it consistently selects a higher proportion of informative samples than baselines, and substantially accelerates RL finetuning, achieving performance comparable or even superior to the rollout-intensive Dynamic Sampling strategy with significantly fewer rollouts [12].

snippets: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning has become a key technique for enhancing the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). However, its effectiveness critically depends on the selection of training data.

When the model consistently answers a problem either correctly or incorrectly, a phenomenon frequently observed during training (Zhang et al., 2025), the reward provides limited optimization signals (Chen et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). For algorithms such as GRPO, this situation causes the normalized advantages to vanish, effectively halting optimization.

A representative state-of-the-art (SoTA) approach is Dynamic Sampling (DS) (Yu et al., 2025), which expands candidate prompt batches, generates multiple responses per prompt, discards uninformative prompts with consistent rewards, and uses the retained subset for finetuning.
The results demonstrate that DPS can accurately predict prompts' evolving solving states and consistently select a higher proportion of informative samples compared to baseline methods.

Leveraging this capability, DPS substantially accelerates RL finetuning, achieving performance comparable or even superior to the oracle rollout-intensive strategy DS with significantly fewer rollouts.

sections.title: Test-time active fine-tuning: the active learning principle beats retrieval
sections.text: Even in test-time fine-tuning — where a pre-trained model is adapted to each individual prompt — the active learning principle outperforms standard practice. Recent efforts in fine-tuning language models often rely on automatic data selection via nearest-neighbor retrieval from large datasets, but this approach is shown to select redundant data, limiting its effectiveness or even hurting performance [13]. SIFT instead selects examples to reduce uncertainty about the model's response given a prompt, explicitly unifying ideas from retrieval and active learning, and it consistently outperforms nearest-neighbor retrieval with minimal computational overhead [13]. The authors frame the two approaches as opposite ends of a spectrum: retrieval selects relevant but potentially redundant data, while active learning selects diverse but potentially irrelevant data — and an information-gain criterion that accounts for redundancy is what works in fine-tuning [13].

sections.title: Why the answer depends on the regime
sections.text: The pattern across the evidence can be summarized by a handful of modulating factors. (1) Prior strength: modern LLMs inherit strong priors from web-scale pretraining that limit the headroom of post-training data-selection strategies; when the on-policy candidate pool is already informative, the added value of active selection shrinks [11]. (2) Budget and scale: with small label budgets — few-shot classification or roughly a thousand instruction examples — the value of selection is large [5][6], but at the million-sample scale, complex selectors often fall short of random selection, and only simple representation-based selection retains a small but real edge [8]. (3) Redundancy: uncertainty alone selects repetitive data; the methods that win combine uncertainty with diversity or an information-gain criterion [4][13]. (4) What is being saved: classical active learning saves annotation cost, but when labels are cheap or LLM-generated the question becomes whether selection also saves training compute — and only the cheapest selectors that beat random even after their own compute cost is counted are worth deploying [2][3][8]. (5) Training dynamics: in online RL fine-tuning, where prompt informativeness drifts as the policy improves, active selection has a clear, measurable benefit [12].

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Does active learning work well when fine-tuning large language models? The answer is conditional. It works well when the target model's prior is weak on the target domain or the label budget is small: LLM-assisted active selection outperforms both traditional active learning and strong few-shot baselines for few-shot fine-tuning [5], and uncertainty-and-diversity-driven active fine-tuning substantially improves the label efficiency of pre-trained model fine-tuning [4]. It also works well in online RL fine-tuning of reasoning models, where actively selecting partially solved prompts accelerates training and yields comparable or superior final performance with far fewer rollouts [12], and in test-time adaptation, where uncertainty-reducing selection beats nearest-neighbor retrieval [13]. It does not clearly work — and often does not — when the model being fine-tuned already has strong priors and an abundant candidate pool: for online preference optimization, active selection offers little to no benefit over random sampling [11], and at the scale of production instruction tuning, many automated selectors fall short of random selection while using more compute, with simple embedding-based selection the best option [8]. For practitioners, the safe default is to treat active learning as a tool for tight label budgets and online, drift-heavy settings, and to benchmark against random and cheap selection baselines before paying for an elaborate acquisition function [8][11].

question: During pre-training, why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?

sections.title: From static word vectors to end-to-end pre-training
sections.text: Before the transformer pre-training era, the embedding layer of a language model was typically seeded with static pre-trained word vectors (word2vec, GloVe), because 'Pre-trained word embeddings are an integral part of modern NLP systems, offering significant improvements over embeddings learned from scratch' in data-limited settings [1]. Those static vectors are context-free: 'Static Word Embeddings fail to capture polysemy. They generate the same embedding for the same word in different contexts' [2], so a word is 'associated with the same embedding, independently from the context in which it appears' [3]. Transformer pre-training changes the role of the embedding layer: instead of a frozen prior supplied by another system, the table becomes one of the model's own parameters, trained end-to-end under the model's own objective — BERT's masked language model, in which the model masks input tokens and 'predict those masked tokens' [1], T5's span-corruption denoising objective [4], or GPT-3's autoregressive language modeling [5]. In this regime, word 'embeddings are randomly initialized by default and learned during training' [6].

sections.title: The standard recipe: random Gaussian initialization of every parameter
sections.text: In modern large-scale pre-training, every parameter — including the input embedding table — is sampled from a small-variance Gaussian rather than loaded from an existing model. OLMo 2 states it plainly: 'In OLMo 2, we initialize every parameter from a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.02' [7]. Gaussian initialization 'has become the de facto standard in contemporary LLM literature' [8], and 'In popular codebases for scalable training [127, 114, 137], the default std is 0.02', with recent frontier models reducing it further (DeepSeek-V3 uses 0.006) [9]. The OLMoE report likewise observes that 'For dense language models, a normal initialization with an std of 0.02 has been commonly used' [10]. This practice persists because pre-training at scale supplies enough learning signal: the models are trained on 'up to 6T tokens' (OLMo 2) [7] and '5.1 trillion tokens' (OLMoE) [10], and in 'a rich learning regime, where the influence of initialization is diminished' [11]. Ablations confirm that the exact starting scale barely matters: ICONE varies the embedding-table initialization scale over {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50} and finds 'performance is robust across a wide range of initialization scales' [12]. At pre-training scale, the particular starting point of the embedding table is thus a second-order detail, and a pre-trained prior buys essentially nothing.

sections.title: The embedding layer is learned for its own model, not inherited
sections.text: The core reason is that a pre-trained transformer's embedding table is not a reusable component but something this particular model must learn for itself. The table is co-trained with this model's own attention and feed-forward layers under its own objective [1][4][5], and the input matrix must 'produce representations useful for the model's internal computations' [13]. Static pre-trained vectors come from a different model, trained with a different objective — implicitly factorizing a word-context co-occurrence matrix [14] — on a different corpus, with a different tokenization, in a different space. The resulting contextualized representation space is qualitatively different: a geometry analysis of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 representations concludes that 'even in the best-case scenario, in all layers of all models, static word embeddings would be a poor replacement for contextualized ones' [15]. Empirically, seeding from an existing model can actively hurt: in one study of T5-based sequence-to-sequence models, 'loading the weights from T5 or mT5 was worse than random initialization', which the authors attributed to the pre-trained table clashing with how special tokens such as [BOS] are handled during training [16]. Even when pre-trained tables are used, they do not cover the vocabulary, and missing tokens are given a random initialization anyway [17].

Weight tying, i.e. sharing parameters between input and output embedding matrices, is common practice in language model design, yet its impact on the learned embedding space remains poorly understood.

The technique became standard practice in transformer language models, adopted by GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), and Gemma (Gemma Team et al., 2024), inter alia.

sections.title: Weight tying: the embedding matrix doubles as the output head
sections.text: In many pre-trained transformers the input embedding matrix is tied to the output projection — 'sharing parameters between input and output embedding matrices' is 'common practice in language model design' [13]. The technique 'became standard practice in transformer language models, adopted by GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), and Gemma (Gemma Team et al., 2024)' [13], although at the multi-billion-parameter scale untying is now common (Llama 3, OLMo 2, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3) [13]. This makes a pre-trained prior doubly awkward for the embedding layer: the tied matrix also serves as the unembedding that turns the final hidden state into vocabulary logits, 'optimizing directly for cross-entropy loss' [13], so a static table would seed the output head with a space never shaped by this network's internal representations. More fundamentally, the tied matrix is effectively re-learned from scratch: 'the shared matrix is dominated early in training by gradients from the output layer and thus receives stronger learning signals from the next-token prediction objective. As a consequence, the shared embedding matrix is shaped primarily for output projection, leaving early transformer layers to operate with input embeddings optimized for a different purpose' [13]. Related experiments show that 'models benefit from specialized input and output embedding spaces' [13]. Tied or not, the embedding table's final form is determined by this model's own gradient flow, not by any inherited table.

sections.title: Why pre-training scale removes the case for a pre-trained prior
sections.text: The historical benefit of pre-trained embeddings was to compensate for limited training data [1]. Modern pre-training has no such constraint: GPT-3 trains 'an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model' [5], OLMo 2 is 'trained on up to 6T tokens' [7], and OLMoE was pre-trained on 5.1 trillion tokens [10]. With that much gradient signal, the embedding table is effectively learned from scratch regardless of its starting point — consistent with the observation that in 'a rich learning regime, where the influence of initialization is diminished' [11] and with ablations showing robustness across the initialization scale [12]. Starting from a pre-trained table would add little information while importing mismatch: the table's vocabulary and tokenization (whole words versus subwords), its hidden dimension, and its geometry are all artifacts of another model, and special tokens such as [MASK] have no entry in any static table and even create a pre-training/fine-tuning discrepancy, since BERT 'uses [MASK] token during the pre-training process, but these token are missing from real data during the fine tuning phase' [18]. The default recipe therefore samples everything, embeddings included, from a small Gaussian and lets the pre-training objective do the work [7][8][9].

sections.title: When pre-trained initialization is still the right tool

Where data are limited, or where a smaller task-specific model is built on a fixed architecture, initializing from an existing model's embeddings remains common practice: 'GloVe [23] is a common choice for the embedding initialization. question: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?

sections.title: Short Answer
sections.text: No. On the evidence in the literature, the 1PPS (pulse-per-second) output of a GNSS receiver is not physically generated by a digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) or line driver whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the clock bias estimated by the PVT algorithm. In the standard architecture, the PPS is a 1 Hz time signal derived from the receiver's internal reference oscillator - typically a temperature-compensated or oven-controlled crystal oscillator, and sometimes a rubidium or chip-scale atomic clock - which is continuously disciplined: a feedback control loop (a phase-locked loop or a PID-style disciplining circuit) measures the offset between that oscillator and the GNSS system time and continuously steers the oscillator so that its pulses remain aligned with the beginning of the UTC second [1][2]. The PVT algorithm's clock-bias estimate is not the mechanism that generates the PPS; it is the error signal that the disciplining loop acts on: the first PVT solution corrects the bulk of the oscillator bias, and the receiver's oscillator is then constantly re-tuned from epoch to epoch [4][7]. No source in the surveyed literature describes a DCO that is hard-reset by the PVT bias once per second; the uniform description is of continuous disciplining of a physical oscillator.

A time signal, or one pulse per second (PPS) signal, is the $1\mathrm{Hz}$ signal with each pulse's rising edge accurately aligned to the beginning of UTC second.

sections.title: Where the PPS Actually Comes From: A Disciplined Oscillator, Divided Down
sections.text: The 1PPS of a GNSS receiver is a time signal: a 1 Hz pulse whose rising edge is accurately aligned to the beginning of the UTC second [1]. It is obtained by frequency division of the receiver's high-frequency reference - for example, 10 MHz divided by 10^7 - and that 10 MHz reference itself is generated by a crystal oscillator that is disciplined to the GNSS signal frequency by a phase-locked loop with frequency multiplication [1]. Because a single oscillator chain is involved, the 1PPS and the 10 MHz output of a GNSS receiver are coherent, i.e., both are derived from the same disciplined reference [3]. Electrically, the PPS is a square-wave output that is buffered, level-shifted, and distributed to downstream circuits; the line driver mentioned in the question is a signal-conditioning stage, not a time source. A GPS-disciplined clock, for instance, provides a 1PPS square wave and a 10 MHz sinusoid utilizing the received GPS signals [9], and in the GECAM satellite the PPS signals from the GNSS receiver are hard-wired from the receiver to the data management board and the data acquisition boards [8]. Typical PPS edge accuracy is on the order of hundreds of nanoseconds - about +/-600 ns (3 sigma) for the GECAM GNSS receiver [8].

sections.title: What the PVT Clock Bias Actually Does
sections.text: In a PVT solution the receiver measures pseudoranges using its local oscillator and solves for four unknowns: the three coordinates of its position and the clock offset Δ between its oscillator and the GNSS system time; the receiver's clock is then adjusted by that Δ [1]. Because the receiver oscillator is a cheap, poorly stable crystal, the clock has to be adjusted continuously: constant tuning is needed because errors in the receiver clock synchronization cause loss of accuracy for the PVT solution [4]. In the PVT flow, once the least-squares solution has converged and is considered acceptable, the time bias adjustment can be applied to the user equipment clock, and the first PVT solution should correct the major part of the bias that was caused in the rough synchronization to GPS/Galileo time [7]. The residual clock-bias uncertainty is exactly what limits time transfer: only the uncertainty of the GNSS clock bias affects time synchronization, and the basis for time transfer functions in GPS-based products is the one pulse per second (1 PPS) signal [10]. In short, the PVT bias is the error estimate that is fed into the clock disciplining; it is not the mechanism by which the PPS is generated.

sections.title: Disciplining Is a Continuous Feedback Loop, Not a Periodic Re-initialization
sections.text: The canonical implementation of this architecture is the GNSS disciplined oscillator (GNSS DO): the output signals of an oscillator (quartz or atomic frequency standard) are disciplined with the help of the received GNSS signals, and its outputs are a standard frequency (e.g., 10 MHz) and a 1 PPS [6]. Off-the-shelf GNSSDOs combine a GNSS receiver, an oscillator, and phase lock loop circuitry in a compact module [5]. The disciplining is continuous: when locked to GNSS, the internal disciplining circuitry steers the stable internal local oscillator towards the long-term average of the GNSS receiver's 1PPS timing output, with a control loop that is often a proportional-integral-derivative controller [2]. In low-cost designs the same loop is implemented digitally: an FPGA or microcontroller measures the time offset (TIE) between the local oscillator and the GNSS PPS and applies a correction - for example, a correction voltage calculated from the TIE is applied to a TCVCXO, or the TIE of an OCXO is measured against the PPS in a loop with an increasing time constant so as to tune its frequency to the UTC scale [5]. In an FPGA-based autonomous GPSDO, a phase lock loop, a data acquisition module, and an adaptive algorithm run on the FPGA to discipline a voltage-controlled TCXO [3]. The decisive argument against a DCO that is re-initialized every second is holdover behaviour: when the GNSS signal disappears, the disciplined oscillator simply keeps running - in the FPGA GPSDO the 1PPS drifts by less than 80 ns (indoor) and 356 ns (outdoor) over 24 h without a GPS signal [3], which is the behaviour of a real physical oscillator that was steered before the loss, not of a DCO that would need a fresh PVT bias every second. Consistently, the short-term stability of a GNSS clock is determined by the quality of its internal oscillator, while the GNSS signal provides the long-term reference [1].

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: The hypothesis - that the PPS is physically generated by a digitally controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the clock bias estimated by the PVT algorithm - does not match the architecture described in the literature. What is true in that hypothesis: (i) the PPS is produced by a local oscillator that is digitally or electronically controlled, typically a voltage- or digitally-controlled crystal oscillator steered by an FPGA or DSP [3][5]; (ii) the clock-bias estimate from the PVT algorithm is indeed the correction that is applied to that oscillator, with the first PVT solution correcting the major part of the bias and subsequent solutions continuously re-tuning the clock [1][7]; and (iii) the PPS is delivered as a conditioned square wave, so a line driver is merely a buffering/level-shifting stage, not a time source [9]. What is not supported is the periodic re-initialization: the disciplining is a continuous phase-locked or PID feedback loop on the measured time offset between the oscillator and the GNSS time, and it degrades gracefully to autonomous holdover when the PVT solution is unavailable [2][3]. A faithful description is therefore: the 1PPS is the divided-down (1 Hz) output of a local oscillator that is continuously disciplined by the GNSS signals, with the PVT clock-bias estimate serving as the (continuously updated) correction signal for that oscillator - not a periodic reset of a digitally controlled oscillator.

question: Have large langauge models been applied to the schema matching problem in databases and are they effective?

sections.title: Yes: LLMs are now a mainstream approach to schema matching
sections.text: Schema matching — identifying correspondences between the elements of two or more database schemas — is one of the oldest problems in data integration. Traditional systems are "categorized into Schema-based (Rahm and Bernstein 2001; Do and Rahm 2002), which utilize schema metadata (e.g., attribute names, types), and Instance-based (Kang and Naughton 2003), which analyze the distribution or patterns of actual data values", and even after decades of work, "matching still requires a time-consuming, manual curation process for complex tasks" [2][9]. Large language models changed this picture quickly. One 2025 study of the area observes that "The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened possibilities for zero-shot or few-shot schema matching" [9], and a survey of data agents finds that "The adoption of L1 data agents for schema matching has progressed from in-context learning to task-specific fine-tuning and integration into multi-stage pipelines, operating on a prompt-response basis essentially" [10]. Narayan et al. (2022) are credited as the first to apply LLMs to the problem, "using straightforward serialization with few-shot settings" [5]. Fine-tuned models followed: Jellyfish "achieved high accuracy by fine-tuning StarCoder, a Code LLM, for schema matching tasks" [9]. A wave of prompt-driven and retrieval-based systems then appeared — "ReMatch (Sheetrit et al. [2024]) serializes column metadata by concatenating elements such as column names, table names, descriptions, and data types into strings, which are then embedded and indexed for semantic retrieval. Similar candidates are retrieved through semantic search and subsequently ranked and filtered by a large language model (LLM)", while "Matchmaker (Anonymous 2024a) iteratively improved matching performance through self-improving LLM programs, and Prompt-Matcher (Anonymous 2024b) proposed a systematic prompting strategy utilizing JSON schema structures" [1][9]. LLMs have also been applied to the semantic-web cousin of schema matching, ontology alignment: KROMA "harnesses Large Language Models (LLMs) within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline" for ontology matching [8], and a LogMap-based system that uses LLMs as validation oracles "resulted in strong performance in the OAEI 2025" [6].

sections.title: How LLMs are applied: prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning
sections.text: Application recipes cluster into three families. First, direct prompting and context engineering: Prompt-Matcher "proposed a systematic prompting strategy utilizing JSON schema structures" [9]; ConStruM "presents a structure-guided framework for budgeted evidence packing in schema matching", using a context tree and a global similarity hypergraph to assemble a compact, query-specific context pack for the final LLM decision [4]; LLMatch "decomposes schema matching into three distinct stages: schema preparation, table-candidate selection, and column-level alignment", with a Rollup/Drilldown optimization for multi-table schemas [3]. Second, retrieval augmentation: ReMatch "serializes column metadata by concatenating elements such as column names, table names, descriptions, and data types into strings", embeds them, and lets an LLM rank the retrieved candidates [1]; KROMA "harnesses Large Language Models (LLMs) within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline" and, "To optimize both performance and efficiency, KROMA integrates a bisimilarity-based concept matching and a lightweight ontology refinement step, which prune candidate concepts and substantially reduce the communication overhead from invoking LLMs" [8]; SMoG "enhances explainability and reliability by generating human-verifiable query paths while significantly reducing storage requirements by directly querying SPARQL endpoints" over a medical knowledge graph instead of using vector retrieval [9]. Third, fine-tuning and hybrid designs: Magneto fine-tunes small language models for cheap candidate retrieval while reserving expensive LLM calls for reranking, and uses LLMs to synthesize the training data itself — "we use LLMs to derive data. Using LLMs, we can add syntactic diversity and capture different representations for column names and their values" [2]; KcMF works without fine-tuning, proposing "two mechanisms, Dataset as Knowledge (DaK) and Example as Knowledge (EaK), to build domain knowledge sets when unstructured domain knowledge is lacking" [5]; the LogMap-oracle approach restricts the model's role — "LLMs are used only in the validation of a subset of correspondences for which there is high uncertainty" [6]. At the system level, an LLM can drive the whole stack: "The target schema is provided as a JSON Schema document specifying attribute names, data types, and attribute descriptions. GPT-5.2 returns a JSON array of correspondences, pairing each source column with its target column or indicating no match" within an automatically configured end-to-end data integration pipeline [7].

sections.title: Effectiveness: benchmark evidence
sections.text: On established benchmarks, LLM-based methods are effective and frequently match or exceed the previous state of the art. On the MIMIC-OMOP healthcare benchmark, Schemora "establishes new state-of-the-art performance, with gains of 7.49% in HitRate@5 and 3.75% in HitRate@3 over previous best results", and its ablations show that "by including a baseline that performs schema matching without retrieval—relying solely on LLM ranking—we empirically highlight the essential role of retrieval in driving performance" [1]. KcMF "clearly enhances five LLM backbones in both SM and EM tasks while outperforming the non-LLM competitors by an average F1-score of 17.93%" [5]. On a new context-stress benchmark (HRS-B) where column semantics depend on surrounding schema context, ConStruM "achieves 0.935 accuracy, compared to 0.503 for ReMatch" [4]. Magneto documents how hard the problem remains — on its new biomedical benchmark, state-of-the-art existing strategies find that "the best technique achieves at most 0.45 of mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and incurs high computational costs" — while Magneto itself is "scalable and attains high accuracy for datasets from different domains" [2]. In ontology alignment, the LogMap system with LLM oracles achieved "the top-2 overall rank in the bio-ml track" of OAEI 2025 [6], and KROMA shows that "integrating knowledge retrieval with context-augmented LLMs significantly enhances ontology matching—outperforming both classic OM systems and cutting-edge LLM-based approaches—while keeping communication overhead comparable" [8]. LLMatch reports that it "significantly improves matching accuracy in complex schema matching settings and substantially boosts engineer productivity in real-world data integration", in settings where manual work meant "a single schema alignment taking up to 500 hours for two experts" [3]. End-to-end, a GPT-5.2-configured pipeline "is able to produce similar results, for some tasks even better results, as the human-designed pipelines", with the LLM configuration costing "approximately $10 per case study, which represents only a small fraction of the cost of having human data engineers perform the same tasks" [7].

sections.title: Limitations: where LLMs fall short
sections.text: The same literature is candid about where LLM-based matching underperforms. KcMF names the recurring failure modes up front: although LLMs "have shown promising results in these tasks, they suffer from hallucinations and confusion about task instructions", with the confusion decomposing into "(1) hallucination, where the LLM generates incorrect deduction from correct evidence at hand; (2) under-matching, where the LLM rejects matching with overly strict criteria; and (3) over-matching, where the LLM over-generalizes the association of the input data" [5]. SMoG motivates knowledge-graph grounding on the same grounds: "While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in schema matching, they suffer from hallucination and lack of up-to-date domain knowledge" [9]. Naive direct prompting skews toward recall at the expense of precision — early work that fed whole ontologies to ChatGPT achieved "high recall on small OAEI conference-track tasks but suffering from low precision" [8]. Capability is model-size sensitive: ReMatch "shows strong results with GPT-4 [1], but performance degrades with smaller models like GPT-3.5 [25], which often fails to capture relational structures" [3]. Context handling is a first-order variable: "even when long-context models are used, LLMs do not always reliably use the right information when it is buried inside large prompts [1, 14], and schema-matching experiments similarly find that increasing prompt scope is not consistently beneficial [20]", which motivates ConStruM's budgeted context packs [4]; and Schemora's no-retrieval baseline shows that a model ranking columns without retrieval underperforms the retrieval-augmented variant, "empirically highlight[ing] the essential role of retrieval in driving performance" [1]. Finally, cost and scale remain structural constraints: large LMs "demand significant computational resources and face context window constraints" [2], which is why practical systems reserve LLM calls for reranking [2] or, in the oracle design, only for "the validation of a subset of correspondences for which there is high uncertainty" [6].

sections.title: Assessment
sections.text: The evidence supports a qualified yes on both halves of the question. LLMs have been applied to schema matching extensively — since the first few-shot application by Narayan et al. (2022) [5], spanning direct prompting [9], retrieval augmentation [1][8], fine-tuning and hybrid small/large-model pipelines [2][9], knowledge-graph grounding [9], and selective oracle-style validation [6]. And they are effective: in their best configurations they set new state of the art on the MIMIC-OMOP benchmark [1], beat the best non-LLM matchers by an average F1 margin of 17.93% [5], reached the top-2 overall rank in the OAEI 2025 bio-ml track [6], and configured a full end-to-end data integration pipeline for about ten dollars per case study [7]. But an unassisted, directly prompted LLM is not a silver bullet: hallucination and under/over-matching [5], missing up-to-date domain knowledge [9], sensitivity to model size (strong with GPT-4, degraded with GPT-3.5) [3], unreliable use of information buried in large prompts [4], and significant compute and context-window costs [2] all surface in the primary literature. The state of the art is therefore hybrid — LLMs supply the semantic understanding while classical retrieval, schema structure, and knowledge graphs supply grounding, precision, and efficiency [2][8][9].

question: Have specialized approaches been developed for providing LLM assistance when people author SQL queries?

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Yes. A substantial body of specialized approaches for LLM assistance when people author SQL queries has been developed, spanning at least three complementary directions: LLM-based autocompletion of queries in the author's editor, interactive natural-language-to-SQL interfaces in which the user iteratively authors and refines a query, and LLM-driven debugging, repair, and optimization of SQL that the user has already written. The motivation for such assistance is well documented: accessing and querying databases 'often requires specialized knowledge of query languages such as SQL' [1], and converting natural-language questions into SQL 'represents a significant advancement in making complex datasets more accessible', facilitating 'both non-expert and advanced users' in extracting insights from data [2].

snippets: In today's data-driven world, databases are the backbone of a number of applications, from social media platforms to financial systems. However, accessing and querying these vast repositories of information often requires specialized knowledge of query languages such as SQL
citations.title: NLI4DB: A Systematic Review of Natural Language Interfaces for Databases

snippets: The ability to convert natural language queries into structured query language (SQL) through natural language to SQL (NL2SQL) technology represents a significant advancement in making complex datasets more accessible. It greatly facilitates both non-expert and advanced users in extracting valuable insights from extensive data repositories
citations.title: XiYan-SQL: A Multi-Generator Ensemble Framework for Text-to-SQL

sections.title: LLM-based SQL autocompletion
sections.text: The most direct form of authoring assistance is LLM-based autocompletion of SQL itself. The flagship system in this area, SqlCompose at Meta, was built because 'previous work on LLMs for SQL is very limited' and had concerned 'the generation of SQL code from natural language specifications', with the authors noting that, 'to the best of our knowledge, no work exists on autocompleting SQL queries'; they argue that while it is tempting to 'cast SQL as just another programming language for existing LLM autocompletion systems', SQL 'is declarative, has formal table schemas, and is often written in a non-linear manner', and 'it is common for developers to jump around nested subqueries and common table expressions (CTEs), such that information in the suffix becomes just as important as information in the prefix' [3]. To address these challenges they developed specialized models on a Llama base: SQLComposeSA, fine-tuned on internal data and database schemas, which 'substantially outperforms Llama by 16 percentage points on BLEU score', and SQLComposeFIM, a fill-in-the-middle model that is 'aware of the context before and after the line(s) that need to be completed' and which 'suggests the correct table 75% of the time'; the authors report that the smaller specialist models 'provides early indications that smaller specialist models can outperform larger general purpose models' [4]. Deployed in Meta's data query UI, the system is 'used on a weekly basis by over 10k users including data scientists and software engineers', with 'less than 1% of users' having disabled it; user feedback highlighted 'completing tedious or repetitive SQL clauses, suggesting boilerplate coding, and help in eliminate the need to remember difficult SQL syntax', while the most significant negative theme, 'table and column name hallucinations, which has been reduced with the release of SQLComposeFIM' [5].

snippets: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have been used extensively on general coding problems [1, 2], previous work on LLMs for SQL is very limited. Related work has been concerned with the generation of SQL code from natural language specifications [3-5], but, to the best of our knowledge, no work exists on autocompleting SQL queries.
While it can be tempting to cast SQL as just another programming language for existing LLM autocompletion systems, there are three main challenges that warrant special treatment for SQL.
SQL is declarative, has formal table schemas, and is often written in a non-linear manner.

When authoring long queries, it is common for developers to jump around nested subqueries and common table expressions (CTEs), such that information in the suffix becomes just as important as information in the prefix.

sections.title: Interactive natural-language interfaces for iterative query refinement
sections.text: A second line of work keeps the human in the loop and treats the LLM as a co-author: the system proposes SQL, and the user iteratively revises it. In a controlled user study comparing 'SQL-LLM, a state-of-the-art NL2SQL system built on the SeekAI platform, with Snowflake, a traditional SQL analytics platform', 20 participants each completed 12 realistic database querying tasks; SQL-LLM 'significantly reduced query completion times by 10 - 30% (mean: 418 s vs. 629 s, p = 0.036 )' and 'improved overall accuracy from 50% to 75% ( p = 0.002 )', and participants 'exhibited fewer query reformulations, recovered from errors 30–40 seconds faster, and reported lower frustration levels compared to Snowflake users' [6]. Behavioral analysis suggested that users of the NL interface adopted 'a more modular approach to debugging, where users trust and refine generated queries rather than rebuilding them entirely', indicating that natural-language interfaces 'facilitate low-friction, micro-level revision strategies, whereas traditional SQL interfaces demand more complete syntactic correctness upfront' [7]. The same study surveys earlier interactive designs aimed at user-in-the-loop query authoring: the DIY system shows users intermediate data results for each sub-query to help them 'pinpoint logical errors'; MISP and DialSQL 'use a mixed-initiative approach, asking follow-up questions to clarify user intent'; and SQLucid 'integrates interactive natural language explanations with visual highlights and direct editability', with 'task completion accuracy rising to 85% compared to 56 - 67% for earlier systems' and a significant boost in user confidence [8]. It also records an important caveat: one comprehensive comparison 'found no significant difference in task completion time or accuracy between users of state-of-the-art NL2SQL interfaces and those writing SQL manually', suggesting that 'for users with SQL knowledge, current NLIDBs do not necessarily offer an efficiency advantage' [9]. Multi-turn work extends the same idea: some systems 'focus on refining SQL based on execution results', including a framework that 'executes sampled SQL queries to select the most accurate translation based on execution risk' and 'a learned verifier estimating query correctness' [10], and DySQL-Bench, 'the first benchmark designed to evaluate large language models under dynamic, multi-turn Text-to-SQL interaction scenarios', which 'captures the evolving nature of real-world database interactions where user intents, constraints, and analytical objectives continuously change over time' [11].

Additionally, participants using SQL-LLM exhibited fewer query reformulations, recovered from errors 30–40 seconds faster, and reported lower frustration levels compared to Snowflake users.

sections.title: Debugging, repair, and optimization of user-written SQL
sections.text: A third line of work assists the author after the query has been written, by diagnosing, repairing, or optimizing it. SWE-SQL frames this as a distinct problem from generation: although LLMs achieve 'impressive results in converting natural language descriptions into SQL queries (text-to-SQL)', 'diagnosing and fixing existing incorrect or suboptimal SQL code presents more complex challenges' in real-world applications [12]. SQLENS provides an end-to-end correction framework in which an error selector 'decomposes the SQL correction task and guides the LLM through iterative fixes (Error Fixer) based on prioritized errors', and an SQL auditor 'selects the better query between the original and revised versions' [13]. A survey of the field describes the vision of compiler-inspired debugging tools that would 'detect potential errors, enable users to examine the SQL generation process and identify mismatches' [14]. On the performance side, LLM-driven index tuning has been evaluated against Microsoft's Database Tuning Advisor: the LLM's approach 'is based on reasonable rule-of-thumb heuristics (Section 4) derived from the world knowledge acquired during LLM's training', which 'may not be comprehensive enough to cover all plan transformation rules built into a modern cost-based query optimizer' but 'can be used to improve query execution' [15].

However, diagnosing and fixing existing incorrect or suboptimal SQL code presents more complex challenges

sections.title: Pre-LLM precursors and broader context
sections.text: This LLM-based work builds on a pre-LLM lineage of specialized assistance for SQL authors. As early as 2018, researchers studying SQL query completion for data exploration noted that 'such a form of SQL query completion has not been studied yet', and that existing help in database editors is 'mostly syntactic': keyword auto-completion and dedicated SQL editors like SQL Complete or SQL Prompt rather than semantic completion [16]. QueryBlazer later proposed 'an efficient, fully-generative query autocompletion framework' that 'employs an n-gram language model at a subword-level' to 'precompute completions prior to runtime', shown to be 'as effective as previous systems with neural language models' [17]. Natural-language interfaces likewise combined autocompletion with translation, with DBPal providing 'real-time auto-completion and query suggestion to help users who may be unfamiliar with the database schema or the supported query features' in order to 'improve translation accuracy by leading the user to enter less ambiguous queries' [18]. Together, these lines of work show that specialized approaches for LLM assistance in SQL authoring have not only been developed but are increasingly deployed at industry scale.

snippets: To the best of our knowledge, such a form of SQL query completion has not been studied yet. In databases, some help is provided for query formulation, but it is mostly syntactic: SQL editors of leading database management systems propose auto-completion of keywords from the SQL Language, as well as dedicated SQL editors like SQL Complete or SQL Prompt.

question: How can I use an hybridization of ontology and machine learning for text summarization ?

sections.title: Why combine ontologies with machine learning
sections.text:
Automatic text summarization is usually divided into extractive summarization, which selects a subset of the most important sentences from the source, and abstractive summarization, which composes new sentences that were not present in the original text [1]. Ontologies enter this picture as background knowledge: in ontology-based text summarization, the key concepts pertaining to the document are identified and sentences are selected based on the predefined concepts of the ontology, and this is particularly useful for domain-specific documents [1]. Human-generated knowledge bases and ontologies in many domains (Wikipedia, YAGO, DBpedia, and others) have opened further possibilities in text summarization [6], and domain ontologies, defined by experts of that domain, have been successfully applied to information extraction, question answering, and e-news summarization [7].

The machine learning side has matured in parallel: in indicator-representation summarizers, machine learning techniques are often used to find the indicator weights [6]; a classical ML approach trains a classifier that identifies, from a relevant set of features, whether a sentence belongs to a reference summary [7]; and the field is commonly organized by the machine learning method (supervised or unsupervised) and the summary type (extractive or abstractive) [8]. The hybridization opportunity is straightforward: the ontology supplies structured, interpretable semantic information about which concepts a text touches and how central they are, and the ML component learns to weight those signals for sentence selection or, in abstractive settings, to generate text over them.

sections.title: Where the ontology plugs in: sentence representation and scoring
sections.text:
The most common plug-in point is sentence scoring. One family of methods identifies the subtopics of the articles of interest by comparing the sentence words to the ontology and then selects the sentences most closely matching those subtopics; Hennig et al. (2008) proposed the same idea with additional ontology features for sentence scoring, namely tag overlap, subtree depth, and subtree count [2]. A closely related recipe maps sentences to concepts in an ontology using multi-label classification and then uses the resulting semantic representation, together with graph-theoretic properties, to select the important sentences [5]. Baralis et al. used a different data source, a Wikipedia-based large open-source ontology, to identify important concepts in documents so that sentences containing them may be selectively extracted [5].

The ontology can also work at coarser granularity. After marking the counts of the nodes in the ontology, second-level nodes with higher counts are selected as the main subtopics of the article, and paragraphs are then ranked by their closeness to the selected subtopics to form the summary [9]. Ontology partitioning is another structural use: partitioning large ontologies based on their structure can serve ontology-based text summarization, because if the text ontology is properly partitioned so that groups of related sentences fall into different clusters, a summary can be produced by extracting the more important sentences from each cluster [10]. Finally, at the document level, an ontology can first identify which documents are relevant to the user's interest, before any sentence selection happens [4].

sections.title: Where machine learning plugs in: learned ranking and generation
sections.text:
Once the ontology provides structured features, the machine learning component decides how to use them. In feature-based extractive summarization, sentence scores are computed as a linear combination of feature weights, the sentences are ranked by score, and the top-scoring sentences are picked up for the summary generation [7]. The weights themselves can be learned instead of hand-set: Particle Swarm Optimization has been used to adjust feature scores with weights obtained from training on document/reference-summary pairs, and a genetic algorithm has been used to approximate the best weight combination for a multi-document summarizer [2]. When reference summaries are available, the natural design is a supervised classifier: a classical machine learning algorithm is applied to identify, based on the relevant set of features, whether a sentence belongs to the reference summary [7].

The same divide-and-conquer works on the abstractive side. The space of ML techniques for summarization is broad, ranging from classical learners to a combination of a Restricted Boltzmann Machine and fuzzy logic for feature extraction in extractive summarization [11]. For abstractive generation, Kouris et al. built a framework composed of three key elements: a pre-processing task, a machine learning methodology, and a post-processing task [3]. The pre-processing task is a knowledge-based approach, based on ontological knowledge resources, word sense disambiguation, and named entity recognition, along with content generalization, that transforms ordinary text into a generalized form [3]. The machine learning step is an attentive encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence model, which is trained on a generalized version of text-summary pairs, learning to predict summaries in a generalized form [3]. The post-processing task then utilizes knowledge resources, word embeddings, word sense disambiguation, and heuristic algorithms based on text similarity methods to transform the generalized predicted summary into a final, human-readable form [3]. Evaluated on Gigaword, DUC 2004, and CNN/DailyMail, this hybrid alleviated the problem of rare and out-of-vocabulary words and outperformed state-of-the-art seq2seq deep learning techniques [3].

Once the Sentence scores are calculated, the sentences are ranked in the descending order of their scores- starting from the highest score at the top to the lowest one at the bottom. sections.title: Three proven hybrid architectures to copy
sections.text:
Three hybrid architectures have been demonstrated end-to-end and are reasonable templates for a new system.

First, ontology-guided topic identification plus ML question answering (OATS). OATS consists of two modules, ontology-based topic identification and user-focused text summarization: it first utilizes an ontology-based approach to identify relevant documents to the user's interest, and then takes advantage of the answers extracted from a question answering model, using questions specified by the users, for the generation of text summarization [4]. The concepts and relations guided by the ontology are extracted from unstructured text through named entity recognition and semantic relation detection, with deep-learning models such as Bi-LSTM CRF doing the extraction work [4]. The split is motivated by cost: manually annotated gold-standard concept graphs are expensive and time-consuming and difficult to extend to a new domain, whereas pairing an ontology with ML extraction avoids the manual annotation [4].

Second, the ontology in pre- and post-processing with neural generation in the middle (Kouris et al., 2021). In that framework, a pre-defined ontology of concepts is utilized for content generalization in the pre-processing phase and for concept matching in the post-processing phase [3]. It is the cleanest published example of the pattern where the ontology normalizes the input and the neural model learns the generation. Earlier ontology-based abstractive systems followed a simpler pattern, extracting concepts or key phrases from a text to create a summary [3].

Third, ontology features as input to a learned sentence ranker. Combine ontology-derived features (tag overlap, subtree depth, subtree count [2]; ontology node counts for subtopic selection [9]) with classical text features, then either optimize the feature weights (PSO, GA [2]) or train a supervised classifier on reference summaries [7]. When no curated ontology exists, Sakhadeo and Srivastava's frequency-filtered entity relationship graph summarizer is the demonstrated fallback: it combines word-frequency based keyword identification with information from automatically generated entity relationship graphs to select sentences, acquiring entity-relationships using linguistic structure instead of pre-existing ontologies [5]. The authors position this against the principled ontology-based techniques (multi-label sentence-to-concept mapping; Wikipedia-ontology concept extraction) that it substitutes when no ontology is available [5].

The concepts and relations guided by the ontology can be extracted from unstructured text through processes known as Name Entity Recognition (NER) and Semantic Relation (SR) detection, respectively.

These NER and SR models are often based on approaches such as a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Conditional Random Field (Bi-LSTM CRF) (Huang et al., 2015), which is a deep learning method involving a type of neural network known as a long short-term memory (LSTM) layer.

However, those approaches are expensive and time-consuming (e.g., domain experts are required to manually review thousands of documentations) and limited (e.g., it is difficult to extend to a new domain).

sections.title: A practical recipe, with caveats
sections.text:
Putting the pieces together, a working hybrid pipeline for text summarization looks like this:

1. Choose the ontology. Use a general resource such as WordNet or DBpedia, or a domain-specific ontology defined by experts, depending on how domain-specific your documents are [3][7].
2. Map the text to the ontology. Extract concepts and relations with NER and semantic relation models (deep learning such as Bi-LSTM CRF is the standard choice) [4], or map whole sentences to ontology concepts via multi-label classification [5].
3. Build sentence features from the ontology: tag overlap with the selected subtopics, subtree depth, and subtree count [2]; at paragraph level, rank by closeness to subtopics derived from ontology node counts [9].
4. Let ML do the ranking. If you have reference summaries, train a supervised classifier on sentence features [7]; if not, optimize the feature weights (e.g., PSO or GA) or fall back to hand-set linear weights over the combined ontology and classical features [2][7].
5. Select the top-scoring sentences and assemble the extractive summary [7].
6. For an abstractive upgrade, follow the Kouris et al. pattern: generalize the input via the ontology and word sense disambiguation, train a seq2seq model on generalized text-summary pairs, and match the predicted generalized summary back to concrete concepts in post-processing [3].
7. If the goal is user-focused summarization, add user questions and a question answering module on top, as in OATS [4].

Caveats worth planning for. Ontology-based approaches are most useful for domain-specific documents, so expect the gains to shrink on generic news or web text [1]. Domain ontologies require expert definition, and manually annotated concept graphs are expensive and do not generalize easily to new domains [4][7]. If no ontology is available for your domain, learning entity relationships from the text itself is a demonstrated alternative [5]. Finally, evaluate carefully: the quality of text summaries is much more subjective than label matching in classification tasks, and good performance on quantitative analysis is not necessarily equivalent to good performance in qualitative analysis, so pair automatic metrics such as ROUGE with human evaluation [8].

question: How can question generation be used to mitigate hallucination in LLMs?

sections.title: Background: why questions are a natural unit of verification
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) are prone to hallucination: during generation they "occasionally produce information that appears correct but is, in fact, erroneous" [1], and as model capabilities improve, these outputs are "becoming increasingly fluent and convincingly presented," making them hard for humans to detect [1]. Factual hallucination remains "a central challenge" for LLMs, addressed by a wide range of methods including retrieval, self-consistency sampling, reflection and revision, and auxiliary factuality detectors [2]. A recurring insight across this literature is that questions are a natural unit of verification: free-form text is hard to audit, but an individual question with a checkable answer can be verified directly, so methods that make a model generate or answer questions turn an ungrounded generation problem into a collection of smaller, checkable ones. This framing matters because even chain-of-thought prompting, which already decomposes inference into sequential subtasks, is "highly sensitive to prompt formulation and does not eliminate hallucinations" [3]: it is the structure of the questions, not reasoning alone, that grounds the answer.

sections.title: Generating verification questions about one's own draft: Chain-of-Verification
sections.text: The most widely studied use of question generation for hallucination mitigation is Chain-of-Verification (CoVe). In this approach, "for a given initial draft response, first plans verification questions to check its work, and then systematically answer those questions as a CoT procedure to gradually guide the model and finally produce an improved revised response" [5]. CoVe is described as "a structured approach that enhances factual consistency through multi-stage reasoning," with four stages: drafting an initial answer, generating verification questions from the draft, answering those questions and synthesizing recommendations, and producing a refined final response [4]. Two design properties do the work. First, the questions are generated about the model's own draft, so verification targets exactly the content that might be wrong. Second, the questions are answered independently of the original response — the CoVe process involves "independently answering these questions to avoid bias" so that errors in the draft can surface instead of being rationalized [6]. Later pipelines fold retrieval into the same loop: in RVR, the LLM "draft an answer, plan verification questions, retrieve supporting evidence, and revise, reducing hallucinations" [7], and TrueBrief likewise characterizes CoVe as a method "where a model refines its responses through a question-answering process" [8]. The question-generation step also does not appear to trade away generative breadth: in a controlled comparison of CoVe against DoLa and RAG across model families and scales, "CoVe enhances the model's ability to generate diverse and original ideas," while the other methods suppress or barely affect divergent creativity [4].

Different hallucination-reduction methods affect divergent creativity in opposite ways. CoVe enhances the model's ability to generate diverse and original ideas, whereas DoLa suppresses it.

sections.title: Question-based self-detection: interrogating the model's own output
sections.text: Question generation also works in the detection direction: having the model interrogate its own output lets hallucinations be localized before an answer is trusted. One line of work adapts CoVe into a self-questioning detector, building on the finding that having a model draft questions about its own answer and then answer them reduces hallucinations [9]. The text-based variant is limited because it treats the whole generated response as one block, even though a single sentence often encodes multiple facts [9]. To fix this, the response is first converted into a knowledge graph of entities and relations, which "allows us to analyse hallucinations at the level of individual facts rather than large text" [9]. Structuring the output this way "activates latent reasoning and reflection capabilities," and on GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Flash across two detection datasets the graph-based self-questioning approach achieves "up to 16% relative improvement in accuracy and 20% in F1-score" over standard self-detection methods and SelfCheckGPT [9].

snippets: CoVe (Chain-of-Verification) (Dhuliawala et al., 2024) shows that having a model draft questions about its own answer and then answer them reduces hallucinations.
While the text-based Self-Questioning method is effective, its main limitation lies in analysing the entire generated response $o_{i}$ as a single block.

To address this issue, we construct a knowledge graph from the generated response (using the procedure in Section 3.1), which allows us to analyse hallucinations at the level of individual facts rather than large text.

We show that structuring model representations with knowledge graphs, which organise facts as interconnected entities and relations (Agrawal et al., 2024), activates latent reasoning and reflection capabilities, leading to substantial improvements in hallucination self-detection performance.
Compared to standard self-detection methods and SelfCheckGPT, a state-of-the-art approach, our method achieves up to $16\%$ relative improvement in accuracy and $20\%$ in F1-score.

sections.title: Internalizing question generation at training time: VeriFY
sections.text: Most question-based mitigation happens at inference time, but the same question-and-answer procedure can be learned as a training objective. VeriFY augments training with "structured verification traces that guide the model to produce an initial answer, generate and answer a probing verification query, issue a consistency judgment, and then decide whether to answer or abstain" [2]. The verification question is the engine of the trace: it is "generated by a more capable model, applying a controlled semantic transformation to the original query conditioned on $a_0$ (e.g., rephrasing or altering the semantic perspective)," with nine strategies spanning rephrasing, logical implication, and temporal variation used to probe the initial answer from different angles [2]. The model then answers the verification question independently, re-answers the original query in the context of the verification pair, and emits a consistency judgment that decides between answering and abstaining. Training requires care, because "naively training on self-verification traces risks reinforcing hallucinated content"; VeriFY therefore uses stage-level loss masking that excludes hallucinated answer stages from the training objective while preserving supervision over the verification behavior itself [2]. Across multiple model families and scales, the result is a reduction in factual hallucination rates of 9.7–53.3% with only a 0.4–5.7% drop in recall, and the learned behavior generalizes across datasets when trained on a single source [2].

A key challenge of such an approach is that naively training on self-verification traces risks reinforcing hallucinated content, as the model may internalize incorrect facts intended to exemplify negative inference and later refuted in a verification trace.

Across multiple model families and scales, VeriFY reduces factual hallucination rates by $9.7 - 53.3\%$ , with only modest reduction on recall $(0.4 - 5.7\%$ , and generalizes across datasets when trained on a single source.

sections.title: Question decomposition for grounded multi-hop answering
sections.text: When the task is answering complex questions rather than auditing free-form text, question generation mitigates hallucination by decomposition: the question is broken into simpler sub-questions, each is answered against retrieved evidence, and the sub-answers are combined. Question decomposition "is a backward reasoning method to improve performance on multi-hop questions that require integrating multiple pieces of knowledge and inferring over them to obtain the answers" [10]. The sub-question approach has a long history — "decompose a complicated question into several simpler sub-questions and conduct single-hop QA at each step" [11] — and its value for hallucination is that every step can be checked against a source rather than the model's memory. Self-Ask "iteratively determines whether follow-up questions are needed and generates intermediate queries. It then retrieves reference provisions and uses the augmented context to produce the final answer" [13], and in the RAG literature the Self-Ask prompt "breaks down a complex question into sub-questions and then prompts the model to answer them step-by-step" [12]. Decomposition also improves the retrieval side: a question decomposition module "decomposes complex, multi-hop questions into simpler sub-questions," letting the retriever "focus on smaller, manageable pieces of information, thereby improving retrieval precision and yielding a more interpretable reasoning chain" [14]. As a best practice, RAGTurk's guidance is to "Break a complex question into simpler sub-questions, retrieve for each part, and aggregate evidence before answering" [15]. Multi-agent systems push the same idea further: SQuAI "decomposes complex questions into sub-questions, retrieve targeted evidence via hybrid sparse-dense retrieval, and adaptively filter documents," and "integrates in-line citations for each generated claim and provides supporting sentences from the source documents" to ensure faithfulness and traceability [16]. The same question-level decomposition has been ported to vision: Pelican identifies hallucination in vision-LLMs "by decomposing the visual claim into sub-claims that consist of questions grounded in first-order predicates," then generates "Python code to answer subquestions with external tools," so each sub-question is verified by an executable program rather than the model's parametric memory [17].

sections.title: Making generated questions themselves hallucination-free
sections.text: The logic applies in reverse when the LLM is itself the question generator: for exam preparation, QA datasets, or tutoring, the generated questions can be hallucinated. For automatic multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, one study identifies "four key hallucination types in MCQ generation: reasoning inconsistencies, insolvability, factual errors, and mathematical errors," and proposes a multi-agent framework that "breaks down MCQ generation into discrete, verifiable stages," with specialized detection agents and a hallucination scoring metric optimized over refinement rounds; on AP-aligned STEM questions the system reduced hallucination rates by over 90% compared to baseline generation while preserving the educational value of the questions [19]. For knowledge-based question generation grounded in knowledge graphs, contrastive prompting offers a lighter-weight fix: prompts containing contrasting positive and negative examples "guide the model in reducing noise and hallucinations in generation," and a chain-of-thought prompt model scores the candidate questions to keep only the high-quality ones; using contrasting instructions and examples together yields "the highest quality of generated questions and improved accuracy" [18].

snippets: In light of the issues of hallucination and knowledge gaps present in large-scale language models when applied to knowledge-intensive tasks, this paper proposes an enhanced question generation method that incorporates contrastive learning. This method utilizes multiple models to jointly mine domain knowledge and uses contrastive learning to guide the model in reducing noise and hallucinations in generation.

Experimental results show that by designing prompts containing contrasting examples, the model's performance in question generation improves considerably, particularly when contrasting instructions and examples are used simultaneously, leading to the highest quality of generated questions and improved accuracy.

sections.title: Question generation for training data: synthetic QA pairs
sections.text: Question generation can also reduce hallucination by shaping what models learn from. Synthesizing QA pairs from documents is a standard fine-tuning recipe, and the faithfulness of the generated questions is an explicit design constraint: "The second challenge involves generating diverse and faithful question-answer (QA) pairs that accurately capture the underlying domain knowledge," and "Simply reusing or repeating synthesized QA pairs can lead to overfitting and degrade downstream performance after fine-tuning" [20]. When the synthesized questions and answers are grounded and well formed, the effect is directly measurable: on multi-hop QA, fine-tuning on "synthesized data improves EM and reduces hallucination across all models, with larger models performing best" [21]. The caveat runs in both directions, though: "LLM-generated QA pairs may introduce hallucinations into the augmented data, which can lead to subtle degradation in model behavior" [22]. Question generation for training therefore mitigates hallucination only when the generated questions — and the answers paired with them — are themselves verified.

sections.title: Open challenges and trade-offs
sections.text: Several limits recur across these methods. First, latency and cost: post-hoc question-verification methods "introduce additional complexity and latency through repeated model or external calls, and operate only after an answer has been produced rather than at generation" [2] — the gap that training-time internalization such as VeriFY is designed to close [2]. Second, abstention is a precision–recall trade-off: "abstaining more can reduce errors, but at the cost of withholding correct answers," so a question-generation-based system must balance factual reliability against answer coverage rather than simply refusing more often [2]. Third, sub-question quality is load-bearing: "The challenge for question decomposition is to ensure each sub-question collects the truly necessary evidence" [11], and poorly generated sub-questions shift the failure mode from hallucination to missed evidence. Finally, when generated questions are used as a training signal, the generator's own errors can propagate: "LLM-generated QA pairs may introduce hallucinations into the augmented data" [22], and repeated reuse of the same synthetic pairs can "lead to overfitting and degrade downstream performance" [20].
