question: How can the integration of GIS spatial analysis techniques with economic modeling improve the accuracy and effectiveness of environmental policy ?

sections.title: Introduction: environmental policy is a spatial enterprise
sections.text: Environmental policy has always been a spatial enterprise, but only recently have the tools to treat it as one become routine. Policy decisions by governmental and industrial organizations increasingly require accurate information about the environment, on the status of, and trends in, basic environmental conditions, in order to develop environmentally appropriate policies. The same body of work cautions that GIS facilities are, to a large extent, descriptive rather than analytical, that the methodology for analyzing the interrelationships between multiple sources of spatial information remains underdeveloped, and that for policy makers and stakeholders to evaluate the range of options, a framework for evaluating the potential impact of alternative policies on environmental and social outcomes is essential [1]. Yet geo-information is still not used to its full potential in the daily practice of policy-making, even though most of the information used in environmental decision-making is spatial information, and although a number of potentially very interesting applications of geo-information for environmental policy-makers are described in the literature, few applications seem to be actually used in policy-making. Organized by the policy cycle, the same review locates the opportunities from policy design, which includes formulating policy objectives, designing policy alternatives, and performing ex-ante evaluation, to policy evaluation, where performing ex-durante or ex-post evaluations indicates the realization of the objectives and can form a start for a new policy cycle [2]. The economic side of the gap is equally clear: spatially explicit values of services across landscapes that might inform land-use and management decisions are still lacking, and quantifying ecosystem services in a spatially explicit manner, and analysing tradeoffs between them, can help to make natural resource decisions more effective, efficient, and defensible [3].

sections.title: Accuracy, part one: capturing spatial dependence and the right units
sections.text: The first accuracy gain comes from modeling how environmental effects propagate across space, rather than assuming they do not. The spatial spillover effects of environmental policy in neighboring areas were rarely considered in earlier evaluation work, which could easily lead to biases in the evaluation results of the policy effects [7]. Spatial econometric models are built for exactly this: in a study of energy consumption in 34 European countries, the Spatial Durbin Model was chosen because it can capture the spatial correlation of dependent variables and the effects of the spatial overflow of independent variables, and the results confirmed that a country's energy consumption depends on its past values and on the consumption presented by its neighbors, corroborating the importance of territorial contiguity in the success of environmental policy [6]. A second accuracy gain concerns measurement: within the modifiable areal unit problem, the Aggregation Problem and the Scale Problem can both produce different research results, and the key problem in economic spatial research is the choice of a set of areal units at the selected level of aggregation, so GIS-based unit construction must be deliberate rather than default [8].

sections.title: Accuracy, part two: valuing non-market environmental goods in space
sections.text: Value transfer techniques are an attractive option for policy-makers facing pressing time and budget constraints when reliable primary valuation data are absent, and the GIS characterization of the valued ecosystems, including built coastal environment, natural environment, and geo-climatic factors, is relied upon for the spatial characterization of those ecosystems and reveals to be extremely significant in explaining the spatial diversity of value estimates [11]. Value transfer, the procedure of estimating the value of an ecosystem of current policy interest (the policy site) by assigning an existing valuation estimate from a similar ecosystem (the study site), has been made spatially explicit: a methodology for scaling up values for changes in the stock of ecosystems at large geographic scales uses a meta-analytic value function combined with spatial data derived from a geographic information system, in which the parameters of the value function include spatial variables on wetland size and abundance, and site-specific ecosystem service values are subsequently estimated using the meta-analytic value function. The method adjusts transferred values to reflect variation in important spatial variables and to account for changes in the stock of ecosystems, an essential correction because as an environmental resource becomes scarcer its marginal value tends to increase, so multiplying a constant marginal value by the change in area of an ecosystem site, as is usually done in scaling up, is likely to underestimate the value of the change [10]. As more spatially explicit valuation information becomes available, value transfer functions estimated from meta-analysis can be tailored to the need of a site- and nature-specific assessment, and spatially-specific value transfer becomes possible, thereby increasing the accuracy of this method [12]. For large-scale assessments the requirement is stated directly: mapping the full set of ecosystem services in large-scale, nation-wide assessments requires spatially explicit, transferable models [13].

sections.title: Effectiveness, part one: locating benefits and costs for targeting
sections.text: Environmental preferences are not uniform in space, and the role of the spatial dimensions in welfare analysis is often underappreciated in the environmental valuation literature. Willingness to pay varies in geographical space with the presence of localised patches of higher and lower values, and hotspots of WTP for environmental improvements tend to occur close to each other in space, regardless of the ecosystem service or the area under consideration, suggesting that there is a 'general formula' when developing locational targeting of environmental policies: there is significant spatial overlap in the benefits produced by different environmental policies, which can help develop better-informed policies by letting environmental managers better target environmental improvements [14]. At the national scale, combining long-term land-cover data with spatial analysis and an econometric model shows that the changes in ecosystem service values had significant spatial heterogeneity, and that national ecological programs have clear effects on the improvement of ecosystems, but that the effectiveness of different policies varies on spatial and temporal scales; identifying hotspot and cold-spot areas of ESV change is a more practical method of testing the effect of implementing related policies and adjusting the direction of programs in the future [15]. Where budgets are limited, the integration pays off in targeting: in a coral reef priority area, a decision analysis integrated spatially explicit biophysical modelling, economic analysis, and an ecosystem service value function to identify the most cost-effective onsite solutions, the greatest level of pollution mitigation benefit per dollar spent, evaluating the value to society of pollution reduction in a given place based on that place's ecological significance and recreational use; the approach is relevant to a broader context of coastal areas which are struggling with identifying pollution mitigation actions on limited budgets [16]. The same logic appears in negative form in agricultural watersheds: despite decades of policy that strives to reduce nutrient and sediment export from agricultural fields, surface water quality in intensively managed agricultural landscapes remains highly degraded. Partly, agriculture-related water quality programs do not sufficiently account for heterogeneity in water quality benefits nor in costs of the management practices they incentivize, so both the level and allocation may be mismatched with the magnitude of the issue, and the lack of a comprehensive, watershed-scale analysis tool has likely resulted in misdirected conservation funding to management actions with limited cost-effectiveness. The integrated, spatially explicit assessment built to close this gap assigned spatially explicit costs to each management action within the candidate watershed and found that wetland performance was sensitive to placement, emphasizing the importance of watershed scale planning to realize potential benefits of wetland restorations [17].

snippets: Nonetheless, the role of the spatial dimensions in welfare analysis is often under appreciated in the environmental valuation literature (De Valck & Rolfe, 2018; Glenk et al., 2020).
Variations of willingness to pay (WTP) in geographical space have been characterised by the presence of localised patches of higher and lower values.
Our results show that hotspots of WTP for environmental improvements tend to occur close to each other in space, regardless of the ecosystem service or the area under consideration.

Contrasting the distribution of local clusters of WTP will allow us to understand whether there is a 'general formula' when developing locational targeting of environmental policies or not: that is, whether there is significant spatial overlap in the benefits produced by different environmental policies.

Therefore, this study can help to develop better-informed policies since, for example, environmental managers would be able to better target environmental improvements if there is regulatory scope for flexibility in targeting of control measures for pollution, or woodland creation.

sections.title: Effectiveness, part two: simulating policy scenarios before implementation
sections.text: Cost-benefit analysis is advantageous because in most cases it provides quantitative outcomes, making it a valuable tool in spatial planning, and some spatially explicit models can perform cost-benefit analyses and aid in analyzing land use options, which support policy formulations. Over the past two decades the application of spatially explicit models in environmental studies has grown massively, due to the increase in spatial resolution, improvements in computer technology, and increased availability of data. One of the main strengths of these models is their ability to perform scenario-based analyses: they can be used to assess multiple scenarios and identify scenarios that provide the optimal ecosystem services, while the main drawback is the limited availability of data impeding the use of the models [18]. A modeling system that could provide regional assessments of future development and explore the potential impacts of different regional management scenarios was built for the future health of the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries, because predicting future environmental outcomes, whether for water quality or quality of life, requires being able to predict the spatial pattern of land-use change. A cellular automaton model (SLEUTH), calibrated on a historic time series of developed areas derived from remote sensing imagery, projected growth out to 2030 under three policy scenarios, and the managed growth and ecologically sustainable scenarios produced growth patterns that were more constrained and which consumed less natural resource land. The model was designed so that it should be policy driven to facilitate discussion and testing of the effects of different land-use management policies, its assumptions, implementation methodology, and results should be transparent to the average citizen, and it should be modular to facilitate the inclusion of additional scenarios; the authors caution, however, that spatial accuracy and scale sensitivity are among the factors that must be further considered for practical application [19]. Other model families make the economics explicit: land use change models have been developed to simulate the behaviour of individuals and the up scaling of this behaviour in order to relate it to changes in the land pattern [21], and the modeling of intersecting wetland-shrinkage and urban-expansion processes combines cellular automata, a cell-based land-use simulation system governed by combining maps of likelihood with spatial interaction effects, with sector-based economic models [20]. Agent-based models push further: in the Ecuadorian Amazon, GIS is used to establish spatial relationships between farms and their environment, while classified Landsat imagery is used to set initial land-use/land-cover conditions for the spatial simulation and to describe trajectories of land use change at the farm and landscape levels [22]. A final caution: the choice of spatial representation can flip the policy conclusion. In a comparison of two spatial scenarios, a spatially explicit, farm-specific scenario in which specific types of farms are modeled at specific locations, and a multirepresentative farm scenario, estimated compliance costs were quite sensitive to the spatial scenario, with riparian buffers more cost-effective than nutrient management under one scenario and the reverse under the other [23].

sections.title: Effectiveness, part three: spatially differentiated instruments
sections.text: Where damages depend on location, efficient instruments should as well. It is well-known that an efficient pollution taxation scheme should charge each source according to its specific marginal contribution to social damages, and to the extent that the social costs associated with certain polluting activities often depend on the geographic area where such activities are taking place, optimal corrective measures should take spatial information into account. Applied work has built on technologies such as Geographic Information Systems, which are now helping environmental economists to collect and use spatial data, and the welfare gains from updating current policies based on this source-specific damage information are shown to be quite substantial. A major practical limitation, however, has traditionally been the technical and administrative costs involved in gathering and processing the needed information, and in some settings market intelligence modulates, and might sometimes substitute for, spatial information [4].

sections.text: Evaluation faces the mirror image of the design problem. Recent econometric work has shown that neglecting spillovers can severely bias treatment effect estimates, and a fundamental challenge in such settings is determining where treatment effects end, that is, identifying the spatial boundary beyond which spillover effects become negligible and units can serve as valid controls. Using 42 million satellite observations of pollution near coal plants, a nonparametric boundary estimator shows that exponential decay underestimates pollution near sources and overestimates decay at distance, while nonparametric methods reduce these errors, demonstrating that flexible, data-driven spatial methods substantially outperform restrictive parametric assumptions in environmental policy applications [5]. Geographic targeting of public investment makes the same point for implementation: the increased availability of disaggregated spatial data in recent years has made analyses of the geographic targeting of project funding possible, and such analyses can help to improve efficiency and maximize the poverty- and inequality-reducing effects of development programs. A study of World Bank projects in 58 countries finds that, once one controls for population, the correlation between the bottom 40 and World Bank funding switches sign and becomes significant and negative on average, which suggests that project funding is concentrated in administrative areas in which more people live rather than in poorer administrative areas [24].

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Three mechanisms recur across the literature. First, GIS-based spatial analysis improves the accuracy of the economic objects policy works with: values, damage functions, and treatment effects are estimated with spatial heterogeneity and spatial dependence made explicit rather than averaged away. Second, it improves targeting: once benefits, costs, and spillovers are mapped, instruments and investments can be placed where they work, and the evidence shows this is often not where intuition or administrative convenience puts them. Third, it improves the policy cycle itself, through scenario simulation before implementation and spatial ex-post evaluation that can start a new cycle. The caveats are equally consistent: data availability and quality, scale and unit choice, and the risk that uncertain maps inflame rather than inform the political process. None of these is a reason to stop integrating GIS with economic modeling; together they define the engineering standards the integration must meet.

question: How do different fairness metrics correlate with each other across various datasets and model architectures?

sections.title: Background: Why Correlations Between Fairness Metrics Matter
sections.text: Group fairness in machine learning has been formalized through a large family of statistics — statistical parity, equalized odds, equality of opportunity, predictive parity, calibration, and their difference- and ratio-based variants — and the literature has accumulated as many as 21 distinct fairness notions [10]. These metrics cannot all be satisfied at once: impossibility results show that, except in special cases, calibration within groups, balance for the positive class, and balance for the negative class are mutually incompatible, that equality of positive predictive value is mathematically incompatible with equal opportunity when the compared groups have unequal base rates, and that statistical parity rules out the perfect predictor whenever group base rates differ [2][3]. Because the metrics conflict at the level of their definitions, a practical question arises: which of them actually move together when models and data change? One line of work formalizes exactly this question, hypothesizing that if correlations between fairness metrics can be specified for a given context (dataset plus model type), practitioners can group positively correlated metrics so that reducing unfairness for one metric in the group also reduces it for the others — while warning that some representatives are negatively correlated, so that reducing unfairness for one group may raise it for another [1].

sections.title: Robust Positive Correlations Within the Selection-Rate Family (SPD, EOD, AOD, DI)
sections.text: The most reproducible empirical finding is that metrics built from the same group-conditioned rates — statistical parity difference (SPD), equal opportunity difference (EOD), average odds difference (AOD), and disparate impact (DI) — are positively correlated with one another across datasets and model architectures. In a study of 17 bias mitigation methods across 8 software decision tasks, Chen et al. find that AOD and EOD have a consistently positive correlation across all 56 task-model pairs, and that SPD and EOD are significantly positively correlated in 34 of the 56 pairs [4]. A 2025 study of eight mitigation methods across 44 tabular tasks, five real-world datasets, and four ML models reports the same result, noting that the SPD/EOD/AOD positive correlation is consistent with previous empirical findings and that each metric shows the same correlation trend with the group-specific selection, true positive, and false positive rates [5]. A study of models published on a crowd-sourced platform likewise found that the (SPD, EOD) and (SPD, AOD) pairs have similar correlations in both of its datasets — an effect the authors attribute to the metrics sharing the same or correlated true-positive and false-positive group rates [6]. Deep network settings show the same stability: across four image datasets (FairFace, UTKFace, LFW, CelebA) with two DNN classifiers and four tabular datasets (Student, COMPAS, Adult, MEPS), the SPD-DI tie is consistently positive and the DI/SPD and EOD/FPR distributions are consistently similar across datasets, so that improving one metric is consistently reflected in the other [7]. Finally, across very different architectures — VGG19 for computer vision, BERT for NLP, and Wide&Deep for recommendation systems — twelve of fourteen fairness metrics exhibit the same fair/unfair behavior in all models, and the statistical-parity-family metrics (statistical parity, PPR disparity, error disparity) are similar across all three application domains [8].

sections.title: Negative and Inconsistent Pairs: When Fairness Metrics Disagree
sections.text: Positive correlation is the norm within the selection-rate family, but it breaks down at family boundaries and under data-specific conditions. In Chen et al.'s study, the exception is error rate difference (ERD), which exhibits a negative correlation, and for the other pairs the correlations vary in direction from one task-model pair to another [4]. A 2026 study of demographic bias in face recognition quantifies this disagreement directly: error-based metrics (FPR disparity, FNR disparity), performance-based metrics (accuracy disparity, worst-group accuracy), and distribution-based metrics (Wasserstein distance between score distributions) can produce contradictory conclusions about the same system, and the authors' Fairness Disagreement Index (FDI) remains high across decision thresholds and model configurations; the disagreement persists for both FaceNet and ArcFace models, which the authors take to indicate a broader limitation of multi-metric fairness evaluation rather than an artifact of a single architecture [9]. Data properties also modulate inter-metric relations: a dataset-independent analysis of the probability mass functions of six popular group fairness measures finds that positive predictive parity and negative predictive parity behave asymmetrically depending on the class-imbalance ratio, which makes high fairness easier to achieve simply due to class imbalance, and that Equal Opportunity and Positive Predictive Parity are more sensitive to changes in imbalance than Accuracy Equality [10]. Across a corpus of 44 datasets and 136 scenarios, absolute metric values vary widely — equalized odds difference and demographic parity difference span the full [0, 1] range across datasets and methods — so metric values rarely agree across datasets even where pairwise correlations do [11].

sections.title: How Model Architecture, Training Nondeterminism, and Task Shape the Correlations
sections.text: Whether correlations are stable across model architectures depends on what is being compared. When comparing metric behavior (whether a model is judged fair or unfair on each metric), the evidence points to stability: the same twelve of fourteen metrics flip between fair and unfair together across VGG19, BERT, and Wide&Deep models in different application domains [8], and the SPD-DI and EOD-FPR relations are preserved across image and tabular DNNs on eight datasets [7]. When comparing metric values or agreement across thresholds, the picture differs: in face recognition, metric disagreement persists across the FaceNet and ArcFace architectures and across decision thresholds [9], and the crowd-sourced platform study found that while the pairs (SPD, EOD) and (SPD, AOD) correlate similarly across its two datasets, there is no pattern in the correlation values more generally, and models specific to a dataset show similar bias patterns [6]. Training nondeterminism adds a further source of variation: Ganesh et al. show that group fairness scores are sensitive to random seeds, hyperparameters, sampling, and train/test splits, that no bias mitigation algorithm is a clear winner once hyperparameter optimization is allowed, and that for many datasets like Adult, COMPAS, and KDD there is a clear trade-off between demographic parity and accuracy, which isn't surprising since demographic parity is not aligned with accuracy [12]. Finally, on the relation to overall performance, Cascaded Debiasing reports that the Spearman correlation between F1 score and the fairness metrics indicates that interventions with high F1 score generally result in poor fairness and vice versa, consistent with the accuracy-fairness trade-off discussed in the literature, and that the correlation coefficient decreases as the number of stacked interventions increases [13].

sections.title: Implications: Using Correlations to Select Representative Metrics
sections.text: The empirical regularities above have been turned into tooling. Anahideh et al. propose a Monte-Carlo framework that, for a given context (a dataset and a model type), estimates pairwise correlations among fairness metrics by indirect perturbation in the model space and then selects a small set of representative metrics, reducing the overwhelming task of selecting a subset of fairness measures to consider for a context to working with the group representatives [1]. A 2024 review notes that these correlations were used to identify a set of diverse and distinct fairness metrics that best represent a given context, creating a subset of metrics that approximately concur [3], and a multi-objective ensemble study reports that the work analyzing correlations among 16 group fairness metrics (Fair1-Fair16) based on model predictions on four datasets led the authors to group the first eight metrics based on the obtained correlations [14]. Practical guidance follows from the cross-study evidence: within the SPD/EOD/AOD/DI family the metrics are highly redundant across datasets and architectures, so reporting all of them adds little [5]; across families — error-rate difference, predictive parity, accuracy disparity — correlations are context-dependent and can be negative, and single-metric reporting is insufficient for reliable bias assessment [9]; and because the absolute behavior of parity-family metrics shifts with class imbalance, that imbalance must be accounted for when interpreting them [10]. A defensible evaluation protocol therefore reports at least one representative from each metric family (parity-based, error-rate-based, and predictive-parity-based), estimates the within-context correlations before relying on proxy relations, and reports the dataset's class and group ratios alongside the metric values.

question: How do external events influence software projects? Explain with a few recent examples.

sections.title: Introduction: Why External Events Reach Software Projects
sections.text: Software projects are open systems embedded in a world of people, platforms, supply chains, and markets, so they are exposed to external events: pandemics, geopolitical conflicts, security incidents, hardware shortages, economic downturns, and new technologies. Contemporary software is "not built in isolation" [11]; modern applications depend on vast ecosystems of third-party libraries, and because "6 out of every seven project vulnerabilities come from transitive dependencies," a security event in one component "can expose numerous other systems" [13]. This layered dependence means an event that starts far outside a project - a war abroad, a bug in a popular logging library, a factory in East Asia - can arrive inside the project as a schedule slip, a staffing change, a reprioritized backlog, or an emergency fix. This report examines how external events influence software projects, drawing on six recent, well-documented examples: the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2021), the global chip shortage (2020-2022), the Log4Shell vulnerability (December 2021), the Russia-Ukraine war (2022-), the arrival of generative AI (2022-), and the 2022-2023 technology-sector downturn.

sections.title: Example 1: The 2020-2021 Pandemic as an Organizational Shock
sections.text:
The most studied external event is the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced a global, overnight experiment in distributed work: "as a novel coronavirus swept the world in early 2020, thousands of software developers began working from home. Many did so on short notice, under difficult and stressful conditions" [2]. Companies "had to support and (in some cases) equip office workers who quickly transitioned to a work-from-home set up," and researchers emphasized that "working from home during a pandemic is not like regular remote work," with "additional difficulties" from closed childcare, inadequate physical infrastructure, and fear of infection [1].

A survey of 2,225 developers from 53 countries found that "the pandemic has had a negative effect on developers' wellbeing and productivity," that "disaster preparedness, fear related to the pandemic and home office ergonomics" mediate the effect, and that "women, parents and people with disabilities may be disproportionately affected" [2]. A two-wave Microsoft study ("with a combined total of 3,634 responses that answered all required questions") found "a dichotomy of developer experiences": the same factors - no commute, proximity to family, time flexibility - were benefits for some and challenges for others, so "some developers flourished working at home, while others did not fare as well" [3]. Repository mining of 100 GitHub Java projects likewise found that "the impact of COVID-19 is not binary (reduce productivity vs. increase productivity) but rather a spectrum" [1].

The event also changed how projects are managed and proved persistent. A global survey of software companies found that "team, agility and leadership are the three most important factors for achieving resilience during the pandemic," and that the shock pushed many firms toward permanent remote work: "In May 2020, Twitter's CEO informed their staff that they can work from home forever," "Dropbox too will let all employees work from home permanently," and "Amazon has stated that employees whose positions allow them to work from home can do so two days a week" [4]. For project management, the pandemic thus acted as an external event that degraded wellbeing and productivity in the short term while permanently restructuring where, how, and under what assumptions software teams operate.

sections.title: Example 2: The 2020-2022 Chip Shortage - Hardware Supply Shocks Reaching Software Teams
sections.text:
External events also arrive through the physical supply chain. The global semiconductor shortage, "considered by many experts as the modern version of the 70's oil crisis," arose when a pandemic-driven demand spike - "people began to work from home, learn on Zoom, and watch shows on Netflix, resulting in a huge increase in demand for laptops and tablets" - hit a chain that "contained already many vulnerabilities and weak points that were merely exasperated by the current situation" [5]. The ripple reached software-dependent industries quickly: "over 169 sectors and consumer lines were affected by the semiconductor shortage" [5]. For computer makers, the shortage "caused lead times to be prolonged by as much as 120 days for some PC models, resulting in price increases in the bill of materials"; "HP saw a 30 percent drop in shipments" of Chromebooks, and "Intel reported a 5% drop in revenue from notebook sales" [5]. The scarcity propagated across the economy - "the 2021 shortage of computer chips caused problems for many automobile producers because several parts they need require computer chips directly or indirectly" [6] - and automotive and embedded software teams were forced to delay features, re-architect for older chips, or reschedule releases; Samsung's Galaxy Note series was canceled outright over the shortage [5].

The same episode shows that preparedness moderates the impact: despite the shortages, Apple's smartphone business grew "due to proactive planning, order placement, as well as hoarding some high-value critical components" [5]. For software projects, the lesson is that hardware availability - a seemingly external commodity - is a real schedule and architecture risk, and that early hedging (locking components, qualifying alternatives) separates projects that absorb the shock from those that stall.

sections.title: Example 3: Log4Shell (December 2021) - A Third-Party Vulnerability Becoming a Project-Wide Emergency
sections.text:
Security incidents in widely used third-party components are another channel. Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) is "a severe vulnerability that was disclosed to the public on December 10, 2021"; it "exploits a bug in the wide-spread Log4j library. Any service that uses the library and exposes an interface to the Internet is potentially vulnerable" [7]. Apache disclosed it "alongside a fix in Log4j library version 2.15.0," and NIST "classified this threat as a critical vulnerability with the highest severity rating"; an impact assessment "estimates that 4% (or 17,000 packages) on the Maven Central were affected, either directly or via dependencies" [7]. Within a day, "the Mirai and Muhstik botnets, crypto miners, and other malware were observed to use the exploit for propagation," and because "the first fix was insufficient and more exploits followed," the incident ran for weeks rather than days [7].

For software projects, the event was a forced emergency. The vulnerability "had a significant impact on more than 3 billion devices and triggered immediate zero-day exploits," and while patches shipped quickly, "full remediation took weeks due to supply-chain propagation and configuration" complexity [8]. "Both vendors and users needed to work together on patches, complicated by the need to first find out where Log4j was being used-a process which took weeks or months for some" [9]. The incident reshaped project practice as well as project schedules: affected organizations "immediately needed to discover which of its applications contained the compromised version of the Log4j library in order to mitigate its risk," and "Organizations with SBOMs identified the vulnerable component in a few hours, contrary to taking weeks to determine their risk" [10]. In other words, an external bug in one open-source library converted many projects' backlogs, for weeks, into an inventory-and-patch operation, and made supply-chain visibility (SBOMs) a standing project requirement.

sections.title: Example 4: The Russia-Ukraine War (2022-) - Geopolitics and Software Ecosystems
sections.text:
Geopolitical events can directly touch the software supply chain, as the 2022 invasion of Ukraine showed. Open-source maintainers, usually the most neutral actors in the ecosystem, took political stances - the researchers document "three cases where world politics has had an impact on a software ecosystem," with "either benign or malignant consequences" [11]. In the best-documented case, "a developer of the JavaScript library node-ipc" - "which is used by the popular vue.js framework" - "deliberately introduced a critical security vulnerability that, for some netizens, would destroy their computers' files." The library, "fetched about a million times a week from the NPM registry," shipped versions that "check whether the host machine has an IP address in Russia or Belarus, and if so overwrites every file it could with a heart symbol"; "GitHub declared this a critical vulnerability, which was tracked as CVE-2022-23812," and the destructive versions were "removed from the NPM registry" [11]. The same maintainer also published the benign "peacenotwar" library, and other maintainers - including one of AWS Terraform modules - added anti-war messages to their projects [11].

The episode also involved platform-level sanctions: GitHub suspended accounts of some Russian developers, later restoring "the missing pull requests, issues, comments, etc. from the Russian developers whose accounts had been suspended," though user profiles were restored without mention of the suspension [11]. The community response was swift and severe - one contributor observed that "the trust factor of open source, which was based on goodwill of the developers is now practically gone" [11]. For downstream projects, the event demonstrated two distinct influence channels: direct supply disruption when maintainers or platforms act, and a lasting shift in the trust assumptions on which dependency management is built. "Compromise of maintainer accounts" is now explicitly listed among the standard attack vectors of software supply chains, alongside malicious packages and tampered build infrastructure [12].

sections.title: Example 5: The Rise of Generative AI (2022-) - A Technological Event Reshaping Practices and Costs
sections.text:
The arrival of generative AI is the most recent example of an external technological event reshaping software projects. "Since the public debut of ChatGPT in late 2022, AI assistants based on large language models have rapidly gained adoption among programmers," and "by the end of 2023, an estimated 75% of developers were using some form of AI-based coding tool in their workflow" [14]. Measured effects are large: one study found that developers "can finish certain coding activities in nearly half the time using generative AI assistance (e.g., writing new code 50% faster, and code refactoring 33% faster)" [14].

The influence runs beyond speed, reaching project practice and economics. New development paradigms - chat-oriented programming, "vibe coding," and agentic programming - recast the developer's role from writing code line by line to orchestrating and supervising AI-generated code, so "issues of trust and accountability in software development are front and center" [14]. In open-source projects, the shift is visible in the code itself: "the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot has redefined software development" [15]. There is also a cost side: industry surveys report "nearly 89% increases in computing costs from 2023 to 2025 largely due to AI adoption," and "many companies have already postponed AI initiatives due to cost concerns" [14]. The ChatGPT release thus functions as an external event that simultaneously changed how code is written, what skills projects must plan for, and what those projects cost to run.

sections.title: Example 6: Economic Downturns and the 2022-2023 Tech Layoffs
sections.text:
Economic events influence projects through funding and staffing. The 2022-2023 technology downturn brought mass layoffs: "more than 157,000 employees in the tech sector were laid off during the first quarter of 2023" [16]. The downturn "allowed employers to reset labor relations in favor of management. These include cutting salaries, imposing greater management control, and implementing layoffs" [17]. At the same time, the World Economic Forum estimated that "the impact of digitalization on jobs is vastly negative, with an estimated 83 million jobs to be lost in the next five years because of technological transformation and only 69 million new jobs to be created" [18].

For individual software projects, such events show up as cancelled or descheduled initiatives, frozen hiring for in-flight projects, re-scoped roadmaps, and - on the labor market - a sudden pool of experienced engineers that other projects can hire. The pandemic's demand-side effect is visible in the same literature: the lockdowns that forced remote work also redirected spending toward computers - "people began to work from home, learn on Zoom, and watch shows on Netflix, resulting in a huge increase in demand for laptops and tablets" - which is why the demand spike hit a fragile semiconductor supply chain [5].

sections.title: Synthesis: Recurring Channels of Influence and Resilience Lessons
sections.text:
Across the six examples, external events influence software projects through a small set of recurring channels. First, the workforce: the pandemic directly hit wellbeing, availability, and productivity - "the pandemic has had a negative effect on developers' wellbeing and productivity" [2] - while economic downturns remove or reallocate people and reset labor relations [17]. Second, dependencies and supply chains: a single vulnerability in one library reached "more than 3 billion devices" [8] because "6 out of every seven project vulnerabilities come from transitive dependencies" [13]; geopolitical action by a single maintainer disrupted a library "fetched about a million times a week" [11]; and chip shortages delayed the hardware that software ships on [5]. Third, markets and priorities: demand spikes and demand collapses reprice components and re-scope roadmaps [5]. Fourth, technology and practice: the arrival of LLMs changed how code is produced and what skills, budgets, and accountability structures projects need [14].

Two implications recur. First, contingency and visibility buffer the shock: projects that could inventory their dependencies in hours (SBOMs) handled Log4Shell far better than those that needed weeks [10], resilient organizations leaned on "team, agility and leadership" [4], and the chip-shortage winner Apple got there by "proactive planning, order placement, as well as hoarding some high-value critical components" [5]. Second, the impact is rarely binary: the same remote-work mandate helped some developers and hurt others [3], and the same pandemic raised and lowered productivity across projects [1]. Treating external events as first-class project risks - with dependency inventories, staffing contingencies, and explicit geopolitical and supply-chain exposure - is the practical synthesis of the recent record.

question: How do large language models like ChatGPT impact the diversity of published scientific ideas?

sections.title: Why LLMs are a plausible threat to the diversity of science
sections.text: The concern that LLMs like ChatGPT could shrink the diversity of scientific ideas has moved from intuition to a formal research question. Cognitive diversity — variation in language, perspective, and reasoning — is regarded as essential to creativity and collective intelligence, and a synthesis of evidence across linguistics, psychology, cognitive science, and computer science argues that as LLMs become "deeply embedded in people's lives" they "risk standardizing language and reasoning" [1]. A structural feature of the current ecosystem amplifies the risk: text generation is concentrated around "a small number of dominant systems", with adoption rates "surpassing those of any previous digital technology" [1]. Researchers building LLM-based systems for scientific idea generation flag the same issue explicitly, warning under the label "Idea Homogenization" that wide adoption of LLMs in research "could reflect a narrower set of perspectives or systematic biases compared to human researchers not using AI assistance" [11]. At the mechanism level, because models are trained to reproduce the statistical regularities of corpora that overrepresent dominant languages and ideologies, their outputs privilege central tendencies "while marginalizing rare expressions" — a convergence that is "not just a convergence in surface-level linguistic form, but a narrowing of the conceptual space in which models write, speak, and reason" [1].

snippets: As large language models (LLMs) become deeply embedded in people's lives, they risk standardizing language and reasoning.
The same few models now generate text for hundreds of millions of users, with adoption rates surpassing those of any previous digital technology

At scale, what begins as statistical pattern learning, though capable of generalization beyond mere mimicry, becomes a generative force that privileges central tendencies while marginalizing rare expressions, alternative reasoning styles, and culturally specific voices.
The consequence is not just a convergence in surface-level linguistic form, but a narrowing of the conceptual space in which models write, speak, and reason
citations.title: The Homogenizing Effect of Large Language Models on Human Expression and Thought

sections.title: What the published record itself shows: a two-million-paper citation analysis
sections.text: The most direct large-scale evidence on published science comes from a study of approximately two million full-text research articles (2021–2024) linked to citation networks [2]. Measuring AI-assisted writing intensity as the share of a paper's text predicted to exhibit LLM-like features, the authors identify a sharp reversal in 2023, the year ChatGPT was released: before 2023, higher AI-assisted writing intensity was weakly or negatively associated with citation disruption, but "beginning in 2023, however, the association becomes strongly positive" — papers with heavier AI-assisted writing are increasingly cited in ways that displace earlier work rather than consolidate it [2]. For the diversity question, the decisive result concerns the knowledge inputs: the positive association between AI-assisted writing and broad cross-field citation breadth weakens substantially after 2023, and the authors conclude that "the post-2023 increase in disruption is therefore not accompanied by a corresponding expansion in cross-field recombination" [2]. Their own framing is that AI-assisted work amounts to "more disruptive work built from relatively narrower knowledge inputs" [2]. The defensible reading is that LLM-assisted research may produce papers whose citation structures look more novel, even as the combinatorial diversity of the prior knowledge actually drawn on — the raw material for genuinely new idea combinations — narrows.

snippets: We analyze 2 million full-text research articles linked to citation networks and show that, after the diffusion of large language models in 2023, AI-assisted writing intensity became positively associated with citation disruption.
At the same time, its association with broad cross-field citation sourcing weakened, indicating more disruptive work built from relatively narrower knowledge inputs.

Beginning in 2023, however, the association becomes strongly positive and remains so in 2024, indicating that papers with higher levels of AI-assisted writing are increasingly associated with more disruptive citation structures.
The post-2023 increase in disruption is therefore not accompanied by a corresponding expansion in cross-field recombination.
citations.title: AI-Assisted Writing and the Reorganization of Scientific Knowledge

sections.title: The language of scientific writing is converging
sections.text: An independent line of evidence asks whether the language of published science itself is homogenizing. Analyzing native language identification (NLI) — how well an author's native language can be predicted from their text — across three eras of ACL Anthology papers (pre-neural-network, pre-LLM, post-LLM), one study finds that authors' linguistic fingerprints are fading: "a consistent decline in NLI performance over time", consistent with scientific writing being pulled toward a standardized English [3]. The same paper documents the spread of "LLM-specific" vocabulary, "such as the overuse of words that include 'delve' or 'showcases'" [3]. The pattern is not uniform across language groups: authors of Chinese and French origin show "unexpected resistance or divergent trends", while authors of Japanese and Korean origin exhibit "sharper-than-expected declines" [3]. Parallel rewriting experiments show the same directional pull at the model level: three frontier LLMs from different vendors push 13 stylometric markers in the same direction — function words and first-person pronouns decrease while vocabulary diversity and word length increase — regardless of prompt, and explicit voice-preserving instructions reduce the magnitude of the shift by roughly a third without reversing its direction [4]. At corpus scale, analyses have already identified "detectable lexical shifts associated with LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications" [4].

sections.title: Ideation experiments: quality gains that come with convergence
sections.text: Controlled ideation experiments give the cleanest causal evidence, though for creative tasks adjacent to rather than identical with scientific writing. In a randomized online study (N = 293 writers), Doshi and Hauser found that access to GPT-4 plot ideas raised evaluators' creativity ratings of the resulting stories — novelty up 6.7% and usefulness up 6.4% — "especially among less creative writers", yet "GenAI-enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone" [5]. Follow-up analyses quantified the convergence: cosine similarity of the stories rose by 10.7% for writers with one AI idea and 8.9% for writers with five [6]. The same quality–diversity trade-off appears in business settings, where Boston Consulting Group consultants using GenAI generated more and higher-quality solutions but with reduced semantic diversity [6], and in a task close to science, where crowd workers summarizing scientific abstracts produced LLM-assisted summaries that preserved more keywords (40.1% vs. 31.2%) but were significantly more homogeneous than human-only summaries (homogeneity 45.6% vs. 27.1%) [6]. A natural experiment on 2,200 college-admissions essays provides a population-level analogue: after ChatGPT's release, essays showed a "deep homogenization" pattern in which lexical diversity rose while the diversity of ideas within essays and the thematic distinctiveness across essays declined [6][7]. A pre-registered experiment on human–AI co-creation (N = 486) found that a model-led mode, in which the LLM proactively rewrites ideas, substantially improved idea quality but reduced idea diversity, whereas a reflective, human-led mode improved quality while preserving diversity and perceived ownership [9]. Importantly, the effect does not disappear when the tool is switched off: in a seven-day lab experiment with 61 students, ChatGPT use produced "increasingly homogenized contents", and this homogenization persisted even after participants lost access to ChatGPT, while their raw creative performance reverted to baseline [10].

sections.title: Important nuances: collective diversity, design dependence, and skewed convergence
sections.text: Several findings qualify the simple story that "AI flattens ideas". In a large dynamic experiment (800+ participants in 40+ countries) in which participants brainstormed after viewing AI-generated or human-generated example ideas, high AI exposure did not change individual creativity but increased the average amount and rate of change of collective idea diversity — in the authors' phrase, "AI made ideas different, not better" [8]. Homogenization also depends strongly on how the tool is used: in an analysis of 6,875 essays, AI assistance erased 70–78% of the variance in cohesion architecture while the plurality of perspectives actually diversified, and more specific prompts reversed homogenization into diversification on argument depth, demonstrating "that homogenization is not an intrinsic property of AI but a function of interaction design" [7]. Finally, the convergence is not toward a neutral center: because models learn from corpora that overrepresent dominant languages and ideologies, their outputs "tend to reproduce mainstream, institutionally validated perspectives and writing styles", creating "an illusion of consensus" that mutes alternative worldviews [1]. On the question of LLMs' impact on the diversity of published scientific ideas, the evidence therefore supports a conditional rather than unconditional convergence: it is strongest when many independent researchers deploy the same models in the same ways, and it can be attenuated or even reversed by varying prompts, personas, and interaction modes.

sections.title: Mitigations, caveats, and open questions
sections.text: Several lines of work suggest the homogenization pressure is manageable rather than inevitable. Generating AI ideation inputs through 10 diverse personas preserved story diversity relative to a human-only baseline, with some evidence of enhancement in one condition, leading the authors to conclude that the quality–diversity trade-off "may emerge from uniform deployment practices rather than from an inherent limitation of GenAI" [6]. Iterative planning and search over external knowledge in idea generation produced 3.4 times more unique novel ideas than the framework-free baseline, attacking the repetition problem at its source [11]. Prompt engineering — particularly chain-of-thought prompting — can substantially improve the diversity of AI-generated ideas [6], and reflective, human-led interaction designs improve idea quality while preserving diversity and ownership [9]. Three caveats matter for the specific question about published science. First, the two-million-paper citation analysis is correlational — identified from within-author, within-field variation — and measures LLM-like text features rather than verified tool use [2]. Second, most ideation experiments use non-scientific tasks (stories, objects, business problems), so extrapolation to published scientific ideas is indirect [5][9][10]. Third, "idea diversity" is typically operationalized as embedding-based semantic distance, which may not capture the conceptual novelty that actually matters to a field [8]. The empirical balance at present: the strongest direct evidence on the published record — narrower cross-field sourcing accompanying more disruptive citations [2], plus fading native-language signals and spreading LLM-typical vocabulary in scientific text [3][4] — points to population-level convergence, while the experimental literature shows that the magnitude of convergence is strongly modulated by how models are deployed [7][8][9].

question: How does doping impact integrated circuit design?

sections.title: Doping as the primary design dial: threshold voltage and the scaling template
sections.text: Doping — in practice, ion implantation followed by high-temperature annealing — has been the principal lever by which IC designers set the electrical identity of every transistor since the 1970s. For MOS devices, "ion implantation was essential for setting channel doping levels for threshold voltage control"; combined with self-aligned poly-Si gates it reduced source/drain–gate dopant overlap, "resulting in faster and more controlled switching speeds and dramatically higher device yields". Robert Dennard's 1974 systematization of the coupled changes in doping and dimensions that follow from shrinking made doping a design science: "Dennard scaling" for MOS transistors, "built on the use of ion implantation to provide steadily shifting junction depths and dopant concentrations as lateral device dimensions were reduced, or 'scaled', provided an ongoing template for design of next-generation transistors and fabrication process conditions". In that template the doping concentration Na scales by the scale factor κ as dimensions and voltages shrink, so each successive process node is in part a new doping recipe; "The key doping step was the use of implant to set the channel doping level for a controlled depletion layer width" and the corresponding threshold voltage. Early channel doping levels (mid-10^16 dopants/cm^3) were "far below the controlling capability of diffusion doping", which is why implantation displaced diffusion, and implantation also changed IC economics because "the ability of implant doping to use photoresist films as patterning masks, replacing the dielectric 'hard masks' used for diffusion-doping, was a fundamental process simplification and positive economic driver" [1].

sections.title: A chip is a family of doped regions: wells, halos, and shallow junctions
sections.text: Modern CMOS IC design amounts to specifying a whole taxonomy of doped regions, each with a distinct electrical job. "Advanced CMOS transistors call for both deep and shallow doping implants": the deep implants "extend to beyond 1 µm and form the CMOS wells with retrograde profiles" and are "used to suppress latch-up effects along with vertical anti-punch-through ('midwell') doping and deep 'triple wells' for SRAM and FLASH devices", while the shallow implants form the source/drain and channel structures. Short-channel control is likewise a doping-design problem: "control of short-channel effects calls for tailoring of the lateral doping profiles with combinations of HALO and Pocket implants to suppress off-state leakage and lateral punch-through". The design space spans energies from ≤1 keV to over 1 MeV and doses from ≤10^11 to ≥10^16 ions/cm^2, a range that "presents a significant challenge to provide adequate coverage in a high-accuracy, fast-response metrology", and the vertical trend has been relentless — from 100 nm junctions at 250 nm production toward 20–40 nm junctions, depths "comparable with the standard deviation (straggling) of a typical implant" and therefore "difficult to produce and to measure" [2]. Over the decades, implantation applications "had grown beyond threshold voltage adjusts to encompass many carefully designed and precisely controlled doped regions in CMOS wells, channels and gate stacks" [1].

These are used to suppress latch-up effects along with vertical anti-punch-through ("midwell") doping and deep "triple wells" for SRAM and FLASH devices. The shallow implants form the source/drain and channel structures.
In addition, control of short-channel effects calls for tailoring of the lateral doping profiles with combinations of HALO and Pocket implants to suppress off-state leakage and lateral punch-through.

The wide range of doping processes used in CMOS fabrication, ranging in energies from $\leq 1$ keV to over $1$ MeV and in dose from $\leq 10^{11}$ to $\geq 10^{16}$ ions/cm $^2$ presents a significant challenge to provide adequate coverage in a high-accuracy, fast-response metrology.

These junction depths are comparable with the standard deviation (straggling) of a typical implant and will be difficult to produce and to measure.

sections.title: The scaling wall: when required doping becomes the design limit
sections.text: As scaling progressed, the doping the design demanded stopped being benign. Because supply voltages were reduced more slowly than dimensions, "a consequence of 'constant voltage' scaling is the increase in channel doping by k^2 rather than the linear, k, scaling with constant field designs", a trend that "will eventually accelerate the conditions that lead to the breakdown of continual scaling and the 'end of the roadmap' for bulk planar CMOS transistors by ≈ 2011" [1]. In the decananometer regime, "the scaling of the bulk MOSFET to decananometric dimensions also demands channel doping concentrations larger than 10^18 cm^-3"; at such short gate lengths "the statistical fluctuations of the doping in the channel introduce an appreciable dispersion of threshold voltages which is an important, fundamental limitation of the bulk MOSFET design", and "large channel doping increases the source-drain junction capacitance, that are comparable to the channel-capacitance in scaled MOSFET, and reduce effective mobility thus degrading the device performance for a given channel length". Taken together, these penalties mean that "the conventional bulk device architectures fail to deliver required CMOS performance for generations with feature size below 45 nm", and they help explain the move to ultra-thin SOI, where "virtually undoped silicon films eliminate the issue of statistical doping fluctuations" and, with source and drain junctions terminating on the substrate oxide, "the corresponding capacitances are greatly reduced" [5]. The mobility penalty is general across devices: "the mobility is degraded when the doping concentration is increased due to higher effective electric field as well as due to impurity scattering", while at the same time "the source and drain resistance must be scaled down in proportion to the channel resistance, which is increasingly difficult as the junction depth decreases" [10].

sections.title: Doping variability as a first-class circuit design input
sections.text: Because dopants are atoms, their placement is statistically random, and that randomness propagates into circuit timing and leakage. In scaled CMOS, "there exists a statistical fluctuation in the number of dopants in the channel, which can be translated into a threshold-voltage variation"; the resulting standard deviation is set by the substrate doping concentration, the channel length and width, and the oxide capacitance, and the effect is "different in every transistor irrespective of their spatial location". Statistical timing analysis must therefore model the random placement of dopants — which "makes every transistor in a die independent in terms of threshold voltage" — alongside the spatially correlated variations of channel length, width, and oxide thickness, because "neglecting any of these effects may result in unrealistic timing information of the circuit" [6]. A second, process-level source of doping variation is implant-induced transient-enhanced diffusion (TED): the source/drain implants "introduce crystal damage" that during activation annealing "serves as a source of silicon interstitials that create dopant transient-enhanced diffusion (TED)"; because the amount of TED depends on the transistor's shape and size, layout differences produce "the difference in dopant diffusion in the channel/halo, and the corresponding variation of the threshold voltage" — in one study of a typical 80 nm nMOSFET, up to 50 mV of threshold shift, 15% on-current variation, and a 6× off-current swing — so that "if these variations are unaccounted for in the circuit simulation, they might cause distorted circuit performance". The design response is co-optimization of implant and layout, for example designing halo implants "such that the threshold sensitivity is close to flat and therefore eliminate layout sensitivity of the threshold voltage" [4].

The effect of random placement of dopants (threshold voltage variation), on the other hand, is different in every transistor irrespective of their spatial location [13].

The algorithm simultaneously considers the impact of random placement of dopants (which makes every transistor in a die independent in terms of threshold voltage) and the spatial correlation of the process parameters such as channel length, transistor width and oxide thickness due to the intra-die variations.

snippets: When creating source/drain regions of a MOSFET transistor, the implants introduce crystal damage. During subsequent activation annealing, the implant damage serves as a source of silicon interstitials that create dopant transient-enhanced diffusion (TED).

Different amount of TED, experienced by transistors with different shapes and sizes of their source/drain area, lead to the difference in dopant diffusion in the channel/halo, and the corresponding variation of the threshold voltage.

Analysis of the layout sensitivity of a typical $80~\mathrm{nm}$ nMOSFET shows that its threshold voltage can vary up to $50~\mathrm{mV}$ between the nested and isolated gates. This leads to Idlin variation of up to $15\%$ and Ioff variation of up to 6 times.
If these variations are unaccounted for in the circuit simulation, they might cause distorted circuit performance.

For each set of design rules/technology node, it is possible to design the halo implants such that the threshold sensitivity is close to flat and therefore eliminate layout sensitivity of the threshold voltage.

sections.title: Process constraints: thermal budget, diffusion control, and metrology
sections.text: Every doped design must survive the anneal that activates it, and that anneal is a global constraint on the whole IC. Ion implantation is "technologically demanding, involving the use of vacuum processing, high voltages and requiring high temperature (>1000 C) annealing for recovery of lattice damage and dopant activation"; as junctions grew shallower, this meant "increasingly constrained thermal budgets to minimize dopant diffusion during damage annealing and activation" and "pre-amorphization implants to suppress channeling effects for light ion (Boron) doping" [1]. More recently, "co-implantation, cryogenic implantation or Cluster implant were developed to reduce the dopant's diffusion in the substrate during activation step", with carbon co-implantation giving "good control of dopant diffusion in both silicon or germanium based transistors" [7]. On the measurement side, doping control is so tight that it drives the metrology stack: in a 180 nm process the drain extension implant is "one of the most critical implants", with "the threshold voltage and several other electrical parameters depend on both the depth and the dose of this implant", demanding metrology that "needs to be sensitive to changes in the junction of 0.25 nm. This is comparable to the width of an atom!" [2]. The heavily doped regions themselves carry physics the design must absorb: "the different mechanisms causing bandgap narrowing in heavily doped silicon are reviewed", distinguishing "many-body effects and the effects due to random impurity distribution", with "experimental values for the minority-carrier lifetime as a function of the doping level" and transport described "in the case of a position dependent bandgap" [3].

snippets: Although technologically demanding, involving the use of vacuum processing, high voltages and requiring high temperature $(>1000\mathrm{C})$ annealing for recovery of lattice damage and dopant activation, ion implantation brought several key advantages to both bipolar and MOS transistor fabrication.

For ion implantation process, the decades of 1970's until 2010 saw a steady, highly predictable, shrinkage of source/drain junction depths, leading to the use of lower ion energies, pre-amorphization implants to suppress channeling effects for light ion (Boron) doping and increasingly constrained thermal budgets to minimize dopant diffusion during damage annealing and activation.

sections.title: Heavy doping at the contacts: the access-resistance trade
sections.text: Access resistance is a key figure in transistor speed, and the design answer has always been extreme local doping: "In silicon CMOS, the contact and spacer regions undergo heavy doping with a concentration ranging from 10^21 to 10^22 cm^-3 to reduce access resistance while keeping parasitic capacitance low, thereby reducing the resistive-capacitive (RC) delay of the transistor". This is the classic doping dilemma in miniature: the same heavy doping that lowers series resistance degrades mobility "due to higher effective electric field as well as due to impurity scattering" [10], shifts local physics through bandgap narrowing and a position-dependent bandgap that must enter the transport equations [3], and matters enough in scaled devices that "the ability to model the effects of doping on the depleted MOS surface velocity is particularly important for scaled devices because of high doping levels and high device susceptibility to generation currents" [11]. In emerging 2D channel materials the dilemma sharpens further: "the reduced screening in 2D semiconductors leads to much larger dopant ionization energy, thus much lower doping efficiency than bulk semiconductors", so "it is imperative to develop controlled and reliable doping techniques for constructing transistors and ICs using 2D semiconductors"; doping remains one of the unresolved issues — alongside "metal contact, dielectric integration, spacer design" — that keep prototype 2D performance below roadmap requirements [8].

sections.title: Doping as an architectural constraint — and a design-out target
sections.text: Looking ahead, doping both enables and constrains new architectures. In the 2D-to-3D transition, the new challenges include "uniform junction formation in fin, and severer layout dependent effect (LDE) on stress" — i.e., doping uniformity becomes an explicit architecture-level requirement [7]. Physical doping's high-temperature activation anneal collides with low-thermal-budget integration, and "with the physical gate length of modern devices approaching 10 nm, ion implantation has become increasingly more complicated to control"; "fluctuations in number of dopant atoms present in the transistor channel are responsible for an increased variability of the threshold voltage", and because "the doping process irreversibly sets the polarity of the transistors (n- or p-type)", demonstrated doping-free alternatives — complementary logic gates built from polarity-controllable 2D transistors — offer "a path to enable doping-free low-power electronics on 2D semiconductors, going beyond the concept of unipolar physically doped devices" [9]. sections.title: Synthesis: doping across the design stack
sections.text: Viewed end-to-end, doping touches every level of integrated circuit design. It is the primary means of setting transistor identity — channel doping for threshold-voltage control — and the variable around which Dennard-style scaling was organized for four decades; under constant-voltage scaling, "the increase in channel doping by k^2 rather than the linear, k, scaling" accelerated the end of the planar roadmap [1]. Scaling has pushed required concentrations up, from ">10^18 cm^-3" channel doping in the decananometer regime [5] to 10^21–10^22 cm^-3 in contacts and spacers [8], where statistical dopant fluctuations, extra junction capacitance, impurity-scattering mobility degradation, and bandgap narrowing all feed back into speed, leakage, and variability. The atomic randomness of dopants makes their placement a first-class input to statistical timing and circuit simulation [6], and the thermal, diffusion, and metrology constraints of doping technology — above all the high-temperature anneals required for dopant activation [9] — set hard limits on which architectures (monolithic 3D, 2D channels, 3D fins) are buildable, motivating process innovations such as cryogenic and co-implantation and device concepts such as undoped thin bodies and doping-free logic.

question: How does in-context learning for LLMs differ from traditional machine learning model training?

sections.title: The core distinction: learning without touching the weights
sections.text: In-context learning (ICL) refers to the ability of a large language model to adapt to a new task at inference time by conditioning on a small number of examples provided in the prompt, without any update of the model parameters [1]. At inference time, 'an LLM is able to learn new patterns without any additional weight update when these patterns are presented in the form of examples in the prompt, even if these patterns were not seen during training' [2]. Traditional machine learning works the other way around: historically, the ability to extract patterns from data 'has been understood as a dynamical process in which model weights are updated through an optimization procedure', whereas in ICL 'the model weights remain unchanged' [2]. The two regimes are often framed as different modes of learning: in-context learning is 'a special case of few-shot learning in which the output is conditioned on examples from a 'context', and where there are no gradient updates', while in-weights learning is the standard supervised setting, which is 'slow (requiring many examples)' and 'depends on gradient updates to the weights' [3].

snippets: In-context learning refers to the ability of a large language model to adapt to a new task at inference time by conditioning on a small number of examples provided in the prompt, without any update of the model parameters.

snippets: One of the most striking features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their ability to learn in-context. Namely at inference time an LLM is able to learn new patterns without any additional weight update when these patterns are presented in the form of examples in the prompt, even if these patterns were not seen during training.

Historically, in machine learning, the ability to extract patterns from data has been understood as a dynamical process in which model weights are updated through an optimization procedure. However, in the case of ICL, the model weights remain unchanged.
Specifically, we show how a transformer block implicitly transforms a context into a low-rank weight-update of its MLP layer.

our work demonstrates that contextual blocks, such as self-attention layers combined with a neural network, indeed perform a sort of implicit low-rank finetuning that can be explicitly described as a rank-1 matrix update of the MLP weights computed directly from the relative effect on the context

metadata.authors: Dherin, B., Munn, M., Mazzawi, H., Wunder, M., Gonzalvo, J.

snippets: In-context learning is a special case of few-shot learning in which the output is conditioned on examples from a 'context', and where there are no gradient updates. It contrasts with 'in-weights' learning, which is the standard setting for supervised learning – this is slow (requiring many examples), and depends on gradient updates to the weights.

In the case of transformer language models, however, the capacity for in-context learning is emergent. Neither the model's transformer architecture nor its learning objective are explicitly designed with in-context learning in mind.

In-context learning emerges when the training data exhibits particular distributional properties such as burstiness (items appear in clusters rather than being uniformly distributed over time) and having large numbers of rarely occurring classes.

standard supervised training typically consists of item classes that recur with uniform regularity, and with item-label mappings that are fixed throughout training – these properties allow a model to gradually learn over time, by encoding information into its weights, e.g. via gradient descent.

sections.title: Where the examples are consumed: prompt versus training set
sections.text: In the classical pipeline, examples are consumed during optimization: even in the LLM era, 'the common approach for applying it to a specific downstream natural language task is to further train it on task-specific data, in a procedure referred to as fine-tuning' [4]. ICL inverts the roles — the same input–label pairs go into the input of a frozen model. Formally, a PAC framework for the setting describes 'an initial pretraining phase, which fits a function to the pretraining distribution, and then a second in-context learning phase, which keeps this function constant and concatenates training examples of the downstream task in its input' [4]. The model then answers by continuation, choosing 'the label y that is the most likely continuation for the prefix p ⊕ x' [4]. Concretely, the model 'takes a prompt P that contains task descriptions, in-context examples, and the test instance as input, and predicts the label by capturing the patterns in the context' [5]. In short, ICL 'adapts the model without altering its parameters, instead providing downstream training samples as part of the input prompt or context' [6]; which regime to use typically depends on 'factors like downstream dataset size, computational resources, and the need for multi-task adaptation' [6].

snippets: In-context learning is a surprising and important phenomenon that emerged when modern language models were scaled to billions of learned parameters.

After an LM has been pretrained, the common approach for applying it to a specific downstream natural language task is to further train it on task-specific data, in a procedure referred to as fine-tuning.

Our framework includes an initial pretraining phase, which fits a function to the pretraining distribution, and then a second in-context learning phase, which keeps this function constant and concatenates training examples of the downstream task in its input.
Given this prompt, the prediction is made by choosing the label y that is the most likely continuation for the prefix p ⊕ x according to the function f_θ.

Our theoretical analysis reveals that in this setting, in-context learning is more about identifying the task than about learning it, a result which is in line with a series of recent empirical findings.

The language model takes a prompt P that contains task descriptions, in-context examples, and the test instance as input, and predicts the label by capturing the patterns in the context.

ICL has two advantages over finetuning. First, it avoids the need for repeated finetuning when the schema is updated or new examples are added. sections.title: How the ability arises: emergence from pretraining, not design
sections.text: A deeper difference is how the learning ability itself comes into being. In traditional ML the training procedure is explicitly designed for the target task. In LLMs, 'the capacity for in-context learning is emergent. Neither the model's transformer architecture nor its learning objective are explicitly designed with in-context learning in mind' [3]. The ability 'stems from the process of general pretraining' [7] and became visible 'when modern language models were scaled to billions of learned parameters' [4]. Crucially, it requires naturalistic training statistics: ICL 'emerges when the training data exhibits particular distributional properties such as burstiness (items appear in clusters rather than being uniformly distributed over time) and having large numbers of rarely occurring classes' [3]. Standard supervised learning, by contrast, rests on different data: it 'typically consists of item classes that recur with uniform regularity, and with item-label mappings that are fixed throughout training', which 'allow a model to gradually learn over time, by encoding information into its weights, e.g. via gradient descent' [3]. Where traditional training deliberately writes task knowledge into the weights, ICL co-emerges from the interplay of transformer architecture, model scale, and pretraining-corpus statistics.
