sections.title: Practical consequences: cost, flexibility, and limits
sections.text: The weight-free design has direct practical consequences. Compared with conventional machine learning methods, ICL avoids 'the complexity of model training and fine-tuning, a well-known bottleneck of conventional ML techniques' and can formulate and solve problems from 'human language instructions' rather than requiring an engineered training pipeline [8]. Its headline benefits are 'the minimal need for task-specific data and the fact that it does not go through any parameter updates or architectural modifications' [9]. GPT-3, for instance, 'surprisingly perform generation tasks from a few examples without any further gradient updates' [10]. For evolving systems, ICL 'avoids the need for repeated finetuning when the schema is updated or new examples are added', and by 'simply adding/removing training examples' it makes it possible to 'quickly manipulate the model's predictions and correct mistakes without re-training' [5]. The limits are equally well documented. Because ICL-based methods 'use only a small subset of the training data as demonstrations', they can trail models trained on the full data [11]. And although a model with no parameter updates 'matches or sometimes even outperforms fine-tuned models' [12], fine-tuning combined with meta-training 'exceeds both MetaICL and fine-tuning without meta-training' [12] — training remains the stronger regime when the task is fixed and data is plentiful.

sections.title: Mechanistic view: implicit inference-time updates versus explicit gradient descent
sections.text: Finally, the two paradigms differ in what 'optimization' means. In traditional training, optimization is explicit, external, and iterative: gradient descent 'is an iterative optimisation algorithm to minimise the objective function J(Θ) over the training data by updating the parameter Θ' [14], and such methods 'iteratively adjust model parameters in the direction of steepest descent' to minimize a predefined objective [13]. In ICL, no external loop touches the stored weights at all. The 'update' is implicit and internal: a transformer block 'implicitly transforms a context into a low-rank weight-update of its MLP layer', and this implicit, per-prompt fine-tuning 'can be explicitly described as a rank-1 matrix update of the MLP weights computed directly from the relative effect on the context' [2]. Some analyses go a step further and argue that ICL is 'more about identifying the task than about learning it' — the task knowledge was already encoded in the weights during pretraining, and the prompt mainly selects which of the learned tasks to run [4].

question: For different modulation types like MPSK, QPSK, and MQAM, I'm measuring the error rate but want to understand and measure the Error Vector Magnitude (EVM) more accurately. I'm using a general equation for all modulation types. Is this the right approach, and what should I expect from the EVM vs. Eb/No curve?

sections.title: One general EVM equation is correct for MPSK, QPSK, and QAM
sections.text: Yes — a single, modulation-agnostic equation is the standard approach. EVM is defined as the magnitude of the vector difference between the measured (demodulated) symbol and the ideal reference point in the I–Q plane [1][2], and the standard way of turning that into a number is the root-mean-square ratio of error power to reference power, EVM_RMS = sqrt( (1/N)·Σ|S_n − S_0n|² / (1/N)·Σ|S_0n|² ), which is the definition in use in IEEE 802.11a [3][4] and the 3GPP metric, where each received symbol is compared with its nearest ideal constellation site [6]. The definition is explicitly constructed to hold across modulation schemes: the constellations of BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM and M-PSK have different amplitude levels, so they are first normalized such that the mean-square amplitude of all possible symbols in the constellation is one, and then the same RMS difference is computed [3][4]. With this normalization, a Monte Carlo study established 'the fact that the normalized EVM is same for all modulation schemes' [3], and a closed-form EVM analysis for IQ imbalance and phase noise found the expression 'independent of the constellation format as long as linear memoryless signals are transmitted', in contrast to BER, which 'is in general different for each modulation scheme' [5]. Cross-standard practice confirms the point: the per-standard EVM computations (WLAN, LTE, EDGE) differ only in which offsets are compensated, and 'in principle each standard uses its own EVM calculation but as seen above, the core principle is the same' [7]. So the modulation dependence is not in the equation: it enters through (i) the ideal point S_0n you subtract, which is the per-format constellation, and (ii) the interpretation of the number, i.e. what a given EVM value implies for BER (Section 3) [3][5].

sections.title: What accurate EVM measurement requires beyond the equation
sections.text: The equation is simple; the accuracy comes from the handling around it. First, compensate offsets before averaging. The standard computation does not merely subtract the ideal constellation — it first optimizes a compensation model (the receiver's degrees of freedom) on the received signal: a constant gain and phase difference, plus time offset, magnitude and phase offsets, and frequency offset in WLAN; the same parameters plus an origin offset in LTE; and additionally a power-reduction-over-time parameter in EDGE [7]. RMS EVM is then the square root of the ratio of the average power of the residual error signal to the average power of the reference signal [7]. This parameter estimation is non-convex, with many local minima around a deep, narrow global minimum, so robust initial conditions are part of accurate measurement [7]. Residual IQ imbalance (up to about 2 dB amplitude and 5° phase are the typical practical upper limits) and phase noise are the main contributors that remain in a real system's EVM [5]. Second, keep the normalization consistent: the scaling constants of the measured and ideal constellations are not the same, so unnormalized values must not be mixed [3][4], and the denominator is the average power of the ideal constellation — 'the average transmitted power for the chosen modulation' — a fixed property of the format, not a per-symbol or peak quantity [8]. Third, choose the ideal reference deliberately: it can be a known reference pattern (data-aided) or the closest constellation point to the received symbol (decision-based, non-data-aided) [8]; at high Eb/No the two agree, at low Eb/No the decisions fail and bias the metric — the non-data-aided EVM-to-BER relationship is trustworthy only for BER < 10⁻² [8]. Finally, average over a large number of symbols; standards even average EVM² over hundreds of bursts (at least 200 for EDGE) [7]. EVM is valued precisely because it needs no data receiver, so it complements the BER measurement you are already doing [7], and it is the more appropriate figure of merit at high SNR, where accurate BER counting would require a very large number of symbols [8].

sections.title: Expected EVM vs. Eb/No curve in an AWGN-limited system
sections.text: In the noise-limited regime the curve is a straight line on a dB–dB plot, with its position set by the number of bits per symbol b = log2 M. Under a Gaussian noise model the RMS EVM reduces to the square root of the noise power relative to the ideal constellation power, EVM_RMS ≈ (N0/Es)^{1/2} ≈ (1/SNR)^{1/2} [3][4], equivalently SNR ≈ 1/EVM² [3], or, in dB, SNR(dB) = −20·log10(EVM(%)/100) [9]. Since the symbol energy relates to the bit energy by Es = log2(M)·Eb [4], the relation against your x-axis variable is EVM(dB) = −10·log10(b) − Eb/No(dB). Three consequences follow. (1) Slope: exactly −1 dB/dB — each 1 dB increase in Eb/No buys 1 dB of EVM improvement, for every modulation. (2) Parallel lines: the curves for different modulations are shifted vertically by 10·log10(b) dB only, so an M-PSK and an M-QAM carrying the same b bits lie on the same line; QPSK (b = 2) sits 3.0 dB above 16-QAM (b = 4), and 16-QAM 3.0 dB above 64-QAM (b = 6). At a fixed Eb/No the higher-order modulation shows a lower (better) EVM because its constellation is scaled up in energy per symbol, and each line crosses EVM = 100% (0 dB) at Eb/No = −10·log10(b) dB, i.e. at roughly −3, −6 and −7.8 dB for QPSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM [3][4][9]. (3) Direct conversion to BER: substituting SNR = 1/EVM² into the coherent M-ary BER expression Pb = [2(1−1/L)/log2 L]·Q{ sqrt[ (3·log2 L/(L²−1)) · 2·Eb/N0 ] } (L = levels per dimension) gives Pb as a function of EVM alone, and the simulated BER-vs-EVM curves for BPSK/4-QAM/16-QAM/64-QAM show the expected inverse relationship [3][4]. A concrete anchor: in a PON system evaluated with QPSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM, EVM was taken as the reference parameter 'since it is easily estimated from the scattering diagrams and it is directly related to the performance in terms of bit error rate', and the required EVM for a target BER of 10⁻³ was reported as about 30% (QPSK), 10% (16-QAM) and 5% (64-QAM), with corresponding required Eb/No of 6.8, 10.5 and 14.7 dB [10]. Note that these tabulated EVM targets are approximate: applying the exact AWGN chain EVM ≈ 1/sqrt(SNR_s) to the stated Eb/No values predicts ≈32%, ≈15% and ≈7.5% respectively, so treat the 30/10/5% numbers as order-of-magnitude design targets [3][4][10]. The important asymmetry for your measurements: the equation is identical across modulations, but the same EVM value implies a very different BER for QPSK than for 64-QAM — that, not the equation, is where the modulation type matters [3][10].

sections.title: Where the curve deviates: the high-Eb/No floor and the low-Eb/No bias
sections.text: Expect the straight line to break at both ends of the sweep. At the high-Eb/No end the curve flattens into an error floor: 'for all three cases, the EVM curve enters an error floor, for which even with increasing SNR the link performance remains nearly constant', and the floor is determined by the system's imperfections rather than by noise [12]. The impairments that set the floor are the usual RF ones — phase noise, I/Q imbalance, sampling jitter, sampling frequency offset, carrier frequency offset and power-amplifier nonlinearity — and several of them grow with carrier frequency [11]. The structure is explicit in the closed-form decomposition: the average mean-square EVM is the sum of a 1/SNR term (the noise contribution, which shrinks as Eb/No grows) plus terms from IQ amplitude/phase imbalance, DC offsets and phase noise that do not [5]. 'The phase noise and the IQ imbalances are the limiting factors in chipset performance' [5], so the asymptotic floor at the high-Eb/No end is exactly the system EVM you want to read off the curve. For your MPSK and QPSK cases in particular, a residual carrier phase or frequency offset rotates the constant-amplitude constellation and appears directly in the EVM — which is why the offset compensation of the previous section is most critical for those modulations [7]. At the low-Eb/No end the deviation has a different cause: if your ideal point is obtained by decision (closest constellation point), the decision itself starts to fail, error vectors are computed against the wrong reference, and the EVM no longer tracks the noise power. EVM is a metric that is 'more appropriate ... at high signal-to-noise ratio' [8], and the non-data-aided (decision-based) EVM-to-BER relationship is trustworthy only for BER < 10⁻²; below that, BER derived from EVM is systematically biased (in one study, underestimated after phase-noise compensation) [8]. If your sweep goes below that region, use a known reference pattern or pilot/training symbols (data-aided EVM) for the reference points [8]; with the true transmitted symbols known, the AWGN straight line in fact continues to hold down to very low Eb/No, with EVM growing above 100% as Eb/No falls [3][4]. One more modulation-specific expectation: at constant mean constellation energy, the points of a higher-order constellation are closer together, so the same absolute error produces more bit errors — the BER penalty of higher-order QAM is much steeper than its EVM penalty, even though the EVM curves themselves are merely parallel shifts [1][3].

sections.title: Practical checklist
sections.text: 1) Keep one equation for all three modulations — the 802.11/3GPP-style RMS EVM with constellations normalized to unit mean-square amplitude is valid for MPSK, QPSK and MQAM alike [3][4][6][7]. 2) Put the average ideal-constellation power in the denominator, with separate scaling for the measured and ideal constellations [3][4][8]. 3) Compensate time, gain, phase and frequency offsets (plus origin offset for LTE-style definitions) before averaging, and use a robust optimizer since the problem is non-convex [7]. 4) Use known pilot/training symbols as the ideal reference at low Eb/No; rely on decisions only where BER < 10⁻² [8]. 5) In the middle of the sweep expect a line with slope −1 dB/dB, with QPSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM on parallel lines offset by −3, −6 and −7.8 dB respectively (EVM(dB) = −10·log10(b) − Eb/No(dB)); a different slope or offset is a sign of a normalization or compensation problem [3][4][9]. 6) Read the high-Eb/No floor as your system's impairment EVM and check it against your oscillator's phase noise and your mixer's IQ balance [5][11][12]. 7) Convert EVM to expected BER with the Q-function relation only in the region where it is valid, and remember that the same EVM is a far worse result for 64-QAM than for QPSK [3][4][8][10].
